activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The force on a charge in an electric field equals the charge times the field strength, F = qE, so doubling the charge doubles the force.
story:
The skate park at dusk smelled of warm concrete and someone's cheap cologne, and Benjamin sat on the lip of the bowl with a physics worksheet on his knee, pencil drifting across the numbers while wheels rattled behind him. He had told his father he would be at the library. That had been three evenings ago, and tonight he had not even bothered with the lie; he had simply packed his bag, walked the eight blocks, and let his father assume whatever he assumed. Addison dropped into the bowl below him, carved once, and came up the opposite wall with the nonchalant air of someone who had never fallen in her life, which was not true, because Benjamin had watched her fall all last summer.

"You're doing homework at a skate park," she said, coasting to a stop near his sneakers.

"I'm computing the electric field strength between two charged plates," he said. "Point P is four centimeters from the positive plate. I have the voltage, I have the separation distance, I divide one by the other, and I get the field." He tapped the paper. "Nine thousand volts across three centimeters. So the field is three hundred thousand volts per meter."

Cristiano arrived then, board under his arm, sweat darkening the collar of his shirt. He flopped down beside Benjamin and peered at the worksheet with theatrical despair. "This is why nobody invites you anywhere. You bring plates with you. Charged plates."

"They're not real plates," Benjamin said. "It's a diagram. But the field is real, in the sense that if you put a charge anywhere between those plates, the field pushes on it."

Cristiano squinted. "How hard?"

And there it was, the question Benjamin had been circling all evening without knowing it. He looked at the next problem on the sheet, the one he had been avoiding: a charged dust particle, of all things, drifting between the plates. He had computed the field himself, three hundred thousand volts per meter, and the dust particle carried some small charge, and the problem asked for the force on it. He had written nothing. His instinct was to say the force was just the field, that the two words meant the same push, and something in him had resisted writing that down all night, the way he had resisted telling his father the truth about the library.

"No, listen," he said slowly, flipping back two pages in his notes, where he'd copied a formula without understanding it. "The force on a charge in an electric field equals the charge times the field strength. F equals q E. The dust particle has a charge, the field I computed has a strength, and the force is the one multiplied by the other." He tried it with the numbers on the sheet. Then he tried it again with double the charge, just to see, because that was the thing his father always said about checking a result from the other side. The force doubled. He sat back. "So doubling the charge doubles the force. Same field, twice the charge, twice the push."

"Congratulations," Cristiano said. "You're excited about dust."

"I'm excited because I was going to write down that the force was just the field, full stop." He crossed out his half-formed answer and started again, the pencil moving more surely now. "And that would have been wrong, and I would have deserved the mark I got."

Ms. Hu, who lived in the gray house across the street and walked the block every evening with her terrier, paused at the fence. She taught chemistry at the high school and had a way of appearing exactly when a person was saying something half-right. But tonight she only raised a hand in greeting, tugged the leash, and moved on, and Benjamin was privately grateful, because he had wanted to work it out himself, or at least to be allowed the illusion that he had.

Addison rolled her board back and forth under her foot, watching him. "So why aren't you at the library? Actually at it?"

He thought about the honest answer, which was that at the library he sat for two hours and thought about the skate park, and here he sat for two hours and actually thought about physics, and that neither of those facts said anything flattering about his discipline, only about where his mind consented to live. He thought about his father, who worked nights and believed in libraries the way some people believed in church, and who would feel, if he knew, quietly disenfranchised, as though the rules he'd set had been voted down without his ballot. "I told him I'd been studying," Benjamin said. "I have been studying. It's just not where I said."

"That's a very small distinction," Addison said.

"It's a distinction," he said. "Whether it's small is the part I haven't decided."

Cristiano stood, dropped his board, and pushed off toward the bowl. "Come argue about it down here where the ground moves," he called over his shoulder. "Bring the dust."

Benjamin folded the worksheet along its crease and put it in his back pocket, the corrected answer still warm in some small way, like a coin he had turned over enough times to see both faces. He stood, took the spare board Addison held out to him, and dropped in.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The FAFSA is the form US students complete to apply for federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and federal loans, and many states and colleges also use it to award their own aid.
story:
Taylor had learned to open her email with her eyes half closed, the way you approach a door behind which a dog may or may not be barking. There was nothing from the university again, only a coupon from a pizza place and a reminder from Mr. Bekele that the FAFSA night for families was Thursday, in the computer lab. She deleted the coupon, kept the reminder, and slid her phone into her boot, where it sat against her ankle all through fourth period like a small hot stone.

Mr. Bekele's classroom had that post-lunch smell of pencil shavings and somebody's microwaved leftovers, and on the whiteboard he had written COLLEGE QUESTIONS in capitals that sagged at the end, as if the marker had gotten tired too. Keagan had claimed the desk by the radiator and was fanning himself with a brochure from a school neither of them could afford. "Look at this," he said. "This one has a climbing wall. If I'm indigent, do I get to climb for free, or do they means-test the wall?"

"Neither," Arian said, not looking up from her laptop. "You fill out the FAFSA and you find out." She turned the screen so the two of them could see the form open behind three other tabs. "My mom made us do it last night. It's the form for federal financial aid, like Pell Grants and federal loans, and our state uses it too for its own aid, and colleges use it for theirs. Everything runs through this one form, and it opens every year, and if you miss the state deadline you're basically setting money on fire."

"So romantic," Keagan said. "You and your mother, one laptop, a single glowing form. That's the plot of a commercial."

"It was midnight," Arian said. "She kept spelling her own name wrong. Not a typo. A different name. Twice."

Taylor laughed, but the laugh caught somewhere on the way out, because she had not done the form. She had meant to. Her mother had said, over dinner, that they would sit down with the computer after the dishes, and then there had been no after, only her mother asleep in her chair with the news still on, and Taylor covering her with the good blanket instead of waking her. That had happened three times now, each time with a different reasonable excuse, and Taylor had begun to suspect the excuses were a kind of artifice, hers or her mother's, she couldn't tell which. It was easier to be inure to the small postponements than to name what they were postponing.

The problem, if she was honest, which she was trying to be, was the numbers. Not the hard ones, the tax ones; her mother could find those in the drawer by the fridge. The number Taylor kept circling was what the university might think they could pay, which was more than zero and less than anything, that strange middle country where you were too poor for the sticker price and too not-poor, on paper, for the full ride. Keagan's joke about the climbing wall was a joke, but it was also a real question wearing a silly hat, and Taylor recognized the style because it was hers.

Mr. Bekele drifted over, hands in his pockets in the way of a man about to ask a question he already knew the answer to. "Taylor. You look like a person composing an argument."

"I'm deciding whether to nag my mom," she said. "There's a state deadline."

"There is," he said, and then, because he was better at this than most teachers, he didn't say anything else. He picked up Keagan's brochure, raised an eyebrow at the climbing wall, and put it back down.

"Come over tonight," Arian said, still typing. "We're basically professionals now. One night, my mom's computer, my mom's terrible coffee. You bring your mom's tax stuff, I'll bring the coffee actually, hers is a war crime."

"You'd do that?"

"I want to watch Keagan try to spell his own street name. It's my whole evening planned."

Taylor took her phone out of her boot right there, which she never did in class, and texted her mother: thursday, arian's house, financial aid form, I found the deadline. It's the one everything runs through. Bring the drawer stuff. Then, after a minute, when the typing dots appeared and disappeared and appeared again, her mother answered: I'll be there. Then: do I bring the good blanket?

That night, at Arian's kitchen table, with Arian's mother narrating the coffee's crimes and Keagan getting the street name wrong twice on purpose and once by accident, Taylor watched her own mother lean toward the screen, glasses pushed up into her hair, reading each line aloud like a woman checking a departure board for a train she'd been told had already left. At the question about income, her mother paused, and Taylor felt the old excuse forming in the room, the sudden memory of an early shift, and said, before it could land, "We have time. We have tonight." Her mother put her glasses back on. Keagan said, "Field five wants your birthday, not your reign," and Arian hit him with a rolled napkin, and somewhere in the noise Taylor's mother typed the date, correctly, the first time.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: In the United States the Federal Reserve's main policy rate is the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves.
story:
The radio on the table behind the cash box said the Fed had raised rates again, and Tyson, stacking tomatoes into paper bags for the third customer of the morning, heard it the way he had heard it all summer, as weather. Slade, working the scale, tilted his head toward it.

"Raised what, though," Slade said. "Like my savings account?"

"Nobody knows," Elijah said from the folding chair, where he was eating a peach over the grass. "They say it on the news like everyone was born knowing."

Tyson's mother owned the stall, and she had left him in charge of it for the whole Saturday because his college orientation included a placement thing in two weeks, some diagnostic that would decide whether he started in the remedial economics section or the real one. He had been reading a photocopied chapter at night, and the chapter kept saying the Fed raises rates to slow inflation, which sounded like a sentence a person could say without anything behind it. He wanted something behind it. He put four dollars in the cash box, gave the customer her bag, and turned the radio up one notch.

The news anchor said "the federal funds rate" and then moved on to weather. Tyson wrote the two words on the back of a receipt with a pencil stub.

"My cousin works at a bank," Slade said. "He's taciturn, though. You ask him a question, you get four words."

"Call him," Elijah said.

Slade called. The market noise made it hard, the honey vendor's bell and a toddler two stalls down, so Slade put the phone flat on the table and set it to speaker. The cousin's voice came through thin and flat. Slade asked which rate the Fed actually sets, since the news never said.

"The federal funds rate," the cousin said. "It's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves."

Slade said thanks and hung up, and for a second all three of them looked at the receipt where Tyson had written the words, as if the sentence might assemble itself there. It didn't. Tyson read it twice in his own handwriting. Banks charged each other. He had assumed the Fed set something a person paid, a mortgage rate, a credit card rate, and the cousin's four seconds of flat voice had disabused him of that in one pass.

"That's it? Banks borrowing from banks," Elijah said. "So when the news says rates went up, it means that one went up, and everything else just follows it around like a dog on a rope."

"I think that's the idea," Tyson said, though he noticed he was saying it with no more behind it than the radio had. He sold two ears of corn to a woman in a sun hat and made change slowly, still working the sentence. The Fed doesn't lend to him or to Slade's cousin's customers. It moves a rate between banks, overnight, on reserves, and somehow that is supposed to reach the price of the peaches Elijah was eating. He could see one half of it: if it costs banks more to borrow, maybe they charge everybody more, and maybe people buy less, and maybe sellers stop raising prices because nobody's buying. Maybe. Every maybe was doing work the sentence wasn't showing.

Ms. Sok, who taught at the high school and kept a stall of cut flowers two rows over, came by for her Saturday tomatoes. She was a stoic about the heat, standing in the full sun in a long-sleeved shirt while everyone else sweated and complained, and she watched Tyson weigh her bag with the pencil still behind his ear.

"You look like a man doing math he doesn't trust," she said.

"Trying to get from banks to peaches," Tyson said, and pointed at the receipt. "The Fed raises this one rate between banks, and they say that slows inflation, and I can almost see the road but there are gaps in it I can't fill. And I can't tell if the gaps are in my head or in the theory."

Ms. Sok paid him, took her tomatoes, and said only that the gaps were probably in both, and that the chapter he'd been photocopying at the library had a hold slip with his name on it that she'd noticed last Tuesday, so he should finish it. Then she was gone into the crowd with her sun hat in her hand.

Elijah finished the peach and dropped the pit into the compost bucket. Slade turned the radio down. Tyson folded the receipt and put it in his shirt pocket, next to the pencil, where it would go home with him and end up, he suspected, taped inside the photocopied chapter, one sentence with the whole weight of the news hanging off it, and a boy carrying it around like a question.

"Same time next week?" Elijah said, already standing.

"Same time," Tyson said, and counted the drawer.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Compound or coating chocolate, which replaces some or all cocoa butter with other fats, sets without tempering but does not have the same snap.
story:
The market smelled of peaches and diesel, and by nine it was already warm enough that Emma worried about the chocolate before she had even unpacked it. She had claimed the corner table beside Mr. Almeida's honey stall, where he let her work in the sliver of shade cast by his canvas awning, and where he charged her nothing but commentary. Her plan was simple and, so far, failing: melt the chocolate, cool it while stirring, bring it back up, dip a knife, and hope it set with the hard shine she had seen in the good bars at the grocery store. Two batches had already gone dull and streaky, bending instead of snapping when she pressed the blade against them, and she had a Saturday crowd to face in an hour.

"You're rushing it," Mr. Almeida said, not looking up from his jars. He had the calm of a man who had kept bees through eleven winters, and Emma found his calm mildly unbearable at seven in the morning.

"I'm following the temperatures exactly." She held up her phone, where a chart showed the numbers she'd been chasing all week. "I stirred the whole time. It still blooms."

"It," he repeated, and smiled at a customer, and handed over a jar of buckwheat honey, and only then turned back to her. "You could do everything right and it still might not cooperate. Chocolate's like that. Some mornings it likes you."

Jadyn arrived at half past nine with an iced coffee and zero helpful instincts. She leaned on the table, peered into the bowl of melted chocolate sweating over a warm pot, and said, "This is so much drama. At the campsite last weekend we just melted the candy melts in a ziplock in hot water and dipped the strawberries and they set fine. Nobody took temperatures. Nobody prayed."

"Those are different," Emma said, but she found she couldn't say how, exactly, and the gap annoyed her. She knew it had something to do with what was in the bag versus what was in her bowl, something she'd skimmed past at midnight in a forum thread full of people arguing about seed percentages. "They're called compound chocolate," she offered, and Jadyn shrugged as if Emma had told her the Latin name of a moth.

"Whatever they're called, they worked."

The third batch behaved differently almost at once. Emma had seeded it with chopped chocolate from the same bar, stirred in slow figure eights, and watched the gloss change from swimming-pool slick to something more like wet paint, and when she touched a smear to her lip it was cool and just barely thick. Mr. Almeida glanced over and said, "There. It's coming together. It wants one temperature, all of it, like your body does." Emma said the chocolate was trying to find its homeostasis, and he laughed harder than the joke deserved, which she suspected was the point of him. She dipped a knife and set it on parchment, and while it set she found herself explaining to Jadyn, in fits, that the candy melts contained other fats in place of some or all of the cocoa butter, that this was why they hardened on their own, no tempering required, and that the tradeoff, as far as she could tell from the strawberries Jadyn described, was the snap. Real tempered chocolate broke. The melts, by Jadyn's own account, had bent.

Jadyn considered this while the crowd thickened, and watched Emma break the test knife's coating with her thumb. The sound was small and clean, like a knuckle cracking, and it left a bright edge. "Okay," Jadyn said. "That's a nicer sound than ours made." She had come to the market intending to buy peaches and leave, and instead she was standing at a folding table at ten in the morning learning that the fuss had a purpose, which she admitted was not the conclusion she'd been hoping for. Emma was already loading a piping bag, wearing the particular fierce look she got when something finally obeyed her, and Jadyn decided the peaches could wait.

Emma sold eleven dipped caramels in the first hour. Two customers asked whether the chocolate was the shiny kind or the waxy kind, and she answered honestly that it was the shiny kind today and that she could promise nothing about next Saturday, which seemed to make them trust her more, not less. She kept a bowl of the failed first batches under the table, and when a small boy knocked one against the table leg and it merely bent, she handed it to him for free and said, "That one's structurally humble."

By noon the table was nearly empty and the heat had won the argument with the shade. The last few caramels were softening at the edges, their shine going cloudy, and Emma packed them into the cooler thinking that the morning's success had been borrowed, not owned. Mr. Almeida, closing his jars, watched her fold the parchment with its ghost-smears of snapped chocolate still bright against the paper.

"Next week?" he said.

"If the chocolate likes me."

He tucked one of the cooled test shards into his shirt pocket, next to the pen, the way a man pockets a receipt for something he intends to come back for.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: In hockey, a saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands on the receiver's blade.
story:
The whistle hadn't even finished its shriek before the pass died on the blade of a defender's stick, and Nolan, standing at the boards with his clipboard, wrote a small tally mark in the column he'd labelled STICKS. By the end of the first drill it held eleven marks. The Grade Nine team he'd been assigned to coach for his community service hours could skate well enough, could shoot when given time, but every pass they attempted across the slot got knocked down flat, like the ice was littered with tripwires nobody could see.

He had planned the drill himself, spread out on the kitchen table two nights earlier while his father washed dishes behind him. Three stations, he'd decided. Passing lanes, give-and-go, a timed circuit. He'd been proud of the neatness of it, the way it looked on paper like something a real coach would run. But watching it now, from the bench where Ms. Santos-Reyes had told him to stand and observe rather than hover, he felt a presentiment that his plan was answering the wrong question. He'd assumed the problem was decision-making, that the kids were choosing bad lanes. The tally marks said otherwise. They were choosing fine lanes. The puck just never arrived.

"You're doing the thing again," Danae said from two rows over in the library the next morning, nodding at his scribbled diagram. She was supposed to be studying for chemistry. "The staring-into-space thing."

"Their passes keep getting blocked. Eleven times in one drill."

"So make them pass faster?"

"That's what I thought. But they're not slow. Ruby timed them yesterday. The passes leave on time." He turned his pen over and over between his fingers. "They just travel along the ice, and any stick in the way stops them. It's like mailing a letter by sliding it under every door on the street."

Ruby, who had wandered over from the printer, leaned down and squinted at his diagram. "You ever see that pass the varsity guys do? The one that sort of hops?"

Nolan had seen it, he realized, dozens of times without ever seeing it. Saturday mornings at the rink with his father, the older players flipping the puck in little flat arcs over sprawled sticks. He'd filed it away as showing off. Now he closed his eyes and tried to recall the shape of it, the way the puck rose, hung flat, came down soft on the receiver's tape.

The next practice, he set up a single station. He dragged two benches onto the ice and laid a spare stick across the gap between them, a low fence of ash and tape. Then he gathered the kids around, their helmets steaming faintly in the cold air of the rink, the way breath gathers around a mug of soup.

"New drill," Nolan said. He held up a puck. "A saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands on the receiver's blade." He rolled the puck off his own stick blade, and it skittered under the laid stick like a mouse under a fence. He tried again, cocking his wrists, and this time the puck rose, travelled flat and level through the air, cleared the stick, and dropped onto the ice with a small clean knock. The kids made the low, appreciative noise that boys that age reserve for things that look like magic.

It did not go smoothly after that. The first twenty minutes were torpid with failure, pucks flipping end over end, landing on their edges, rattling off the boards. One kid named only on his jersey as SORENSEN managed to launch one clean over the glass and into the empty third row of seats. Nolan's instinct, inherited from every coach he'd ever had, was to make them skate laps for sloppiness. He raised the whistle to his mouth and then lowered it, because he remembered, with a small internal flinch, the September he'd spent doing laps for a coach who punished what he hadn't yet taught. He was acclimating to the idea that the drill was his responsibility, not theirs. "Closer together," he called instead. "Start closer, then back off."

By the end of the hour the smallest kid on the team, the one who'd been benched for the last game, lofted a saucer over the laid stick with the puck spinning flat as a coin, and it landed square on Sorensen's blade in stride, and Sorensen one-timed it into the empty net before the goalie had even set his feet. The rink noise that followed was not the magic-appreciation hum. It was shouting.

Ms. Santos-Reyes came down from the office walkway as the kids were stacking the benches. She had watched the whole hour, Nolan knew, without once intervening, which was its own kind of instruction. "Where did that come from?" she asked, nodding at the laid stick, still lying across the gap like a small bridge.

"A friend mentioned it. Then I watched some film of the varsity team. I'd seen it a hundred times and never actually thought about why they did it."

"And the laps you almost made them skate?"

He looked at her, deciding how honest to be. "I used to think you drilled mistakes out of people. Skate till it's fixed." He pulled his gloves off, finger by finger, and the cold bit at his wet hands. "Now I think half the time they're not making a mistake. They just don't have the tool yet, and nobody's handed it to them." He paused, watching the smallest kid demonstrate his saucer to Sorensen again in slow motion, mouthing the motion of the wrists. "Although I could be wrong about the other half."

Ms. Santos-Reyes smiled at that, and picked up the far end of the bench to carry it off the ice.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In C major the dominant seventh chord is G7, made of the notes G, B, D and F, and it pulls strongly toward the C major chord.
story:
Kale's dining table had been cleared of everything except manuscript paper, a pencil with no eraser, and a keyboard whose stand wobbled when you touched it. Elliot sat with his left hand hovering over the keys, not pressing anything, the way you might hover over a word you couldn't spell.

"Sixteen bars," Kale said, dropping into the chair across from him. "Mr. Mori said chord changes. He didn't say how many."

"He said it has to end somewhere." Elliot had been thinking about that all week. His father, who taught jurisprudence at the university, liked to say that endings were easy, that anything could be closed with enough force. Elliot had begun to suspect that music worked differently, that a bad ending didn't close anything at all. It just stopped.

He played what he had so far. Eight bars, mostly C and F, a melody that wandered above them like someone looking for a room in an unfamiliar house. Kale listened with his chin on his fist. He had a way of being scathing without saying anything, just letting one eyebrow do the work, and both eyebrows were up now.

"It doesn't sound finished," Kale said. "Even the half of it that's supposed to sound unfinished."

"I know." Elliot played the last two bars again, the melody climbing to E and sitting there, waiting. Waiting for what, though? That was the part he couldn't hear yet. There was a sound in his head, a specific tension that songs on the radio made just before the end, a kind of leaning, and he didn't know its recipe.

He reached over and built a chord under his melody the way he'd been doing all afternoon, stacking G and B and D. He played the pair, G major then C major, then frowned. Close. Something missing. The chord was polite when he wanted it to be urgent.

On the manuscript paper he had written, in the bar before the final one, the notes G, B, and D. He looked at them a long moment, then at the keyboard, then added one more note to the stack with his thumb. F. He played it. G, B, D, F, and then C major.

The ending pulled. That was the only word for it. The melody note he'd left hanging on E now sounded like it was being drawn home, and the C major chord arrived like a door swinging shut on its own weight. He played it four more times, each time slower, trying to notice exactly where the pull lived. In his thumb? In the B and F grinding against each other somewhere in the middle of the chord? He couldn't isolate it, and the failure to isolate it was somehow the best part.

"What is that?" Kale said, sitting up.

"I added F to the G chord. That's all. One note." Elliot picked up the pencil and wrote the F in, stem down, careful with the spacing. "Somebody told me once, I think it was a video, that in C major the dominant seventh chord is G7, made of the notes G, B, D and F, and it pulls strongly toward the C major chord."

"So that's a real thing. It has a name."

"It has a whole system, probably." He laughed a little. "I found one door in it."

He thought of his father again, then, the way his old man liked to argue that everything worth knowing could be reasoned out from first principles, and the way his piano teacher had once told him that theory was just a description of what ears had already decided. Sitting here with the chord still ringing in his hands, he couldn't fully side with either of them. The note had worked before he understood it; the name had come after the sound; and yet without the name he might never have gone looking for the F at all. Which came first, the hearing or the map? He honestly didn't know, and he found he liked not knowing, the way he liked the space between the seventh chord and the chord it wanted.

"Write the rest," Kale said. "You've got eight bars and a good ending. It's the middle that's a mess."

Elliot spread the manuscript paper flat and smoothed the crease with the side of his hand, as if the gesture could suture the two halves of the page together, the half he'd written blindly and the half he was about to write knowing what he was listening for. He played the G7 again, just to feel it lean.

"Bar nine," he said, and put the pencil to the paper.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: ProPublica, founded in 2007 as a nonprofit newsroom funded by donations, became the first online news source to win a Pulitzer Prize, in 2010.
story:
Rachel set her fork down beside her plate and slid a printout across the table, past the salad bowl, until it touched her father's placemat. "It's the budget proposal for the paper," she said. "We vote on it Thursday."

Her father picked it up with one hand and kept eating with the other. Her mother leaned over to read upside down. The kitchen smelled of the roast chicken that was going cold while they argued, which they had begun to do, quietly, the way they did most things.

The proposal was Khalil's. He wanted the student paper to drop its advertisements, the two hundred dollars a month they got from the tutoring center and the pizza place on Marsh Street, and replace the money with donations from families. Ms. Morin, their adviser, had let him put it on the agenda without comment, which everyone knew meant she wanted them to fight it out themselves.

"So who gives the donations?" her father asked.

"Whoever wants to. Parents, mostly."

"And what do they want for it?"

"Nothing. That's the point." Rachel heard how thin it sounded and kept going anyway. "The pizza place pulled its ad last spring when we ran the piece about health inspections. Khalil thinks if nobody buys anything from us, nobody can take anything away."

Her father put the printout down. He worked in marketing, a fact that had sat between them at this table for years, unremarked until something like this arrived. "The pizza place is a business," he said. "It has interests. But parents have interests too. They want the school to look good. They want their kids' names in nice stories."

"You think donors are worse than advertisers?"

"I think money is money. I think people who give it expect something, even if the something is just goodwill."

Rachel turned her fork over on her plate. In September, before any of this, she had sat in the library with Kassidy doing exactly what her father was doing now, listing the ways the paper had gone soft: the flattering profile of the principal, the buried item about the bus route cuts. Kassidy had blamed it on the ads and then, in the same breath, on Ms. Morin, and Rachel had sat there realizing she didn't agree with either half. The paper was timid for reasons she couldn't name yet, and naming them wrong bothered her more than not naming them at all.

That night she stayed up with her laptop open on her bed, past the point where the house went quiet. She was looking for examples, some model of what Khalil was proposing, and she found one she hadn't expected: ProPublica, a newsroom founded in 2007 as a nonprofit funded by donations, which had won a Pulitzer Prize in 2010, the first online news source to do it. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, copying it into her notes. It was one data point. It didn't prove donations made a newsroom independent, and she could already hear her father asking who donated, and how much, and whether a nonprofit that lived on goodwill could afford to disenfranchise its largest supporters with an unflattering story. She wrote that question down too, next to the fact, because leaving it out felt like cheating.

At Thursday's meeting the room was full and too warm. Khalil presented his proposal with the confidence of someone who had never watched a donor's face change. Kassidy seconded it before he finished. When Ms. Morin opened the floor, Rachel raised her hand and stood, holding her notebook.

"ProPublica was founded in 2007 as a nonprofit newsroom funded by donations," she said, "and it won a Pulitzer in 2010, the first online news source to do that."

"So it works," Khalil said.

"It worked once, that way, that I know of. It doesn't tell us who paid for the rest, or what they expected." She looked at Kassidy, then back at the page. "My dad says donors have interests like anyone else. I think he's right about that and wrong about what follows from it. An advertiser spends money to reach our readers. A donor, at worst, spends money to feel good about us. Those aren't the same leash, even if both are leashes."

"Then you're for it," Khalil said.

"I'm for trying it for a year. With a rule that we publish every donation over fifty dollars, so readers can judge for themselves." She paused. "And I don't know if that's enough. I'd rather say that out loud than pretend I'm sure."

The vote came after ten more minutes of argument. It passed, fourteen to nine, with the disclosure rule attached, and the amendment was hers. Afterward Khalil shook her hand across the row of desks like they had concluded a treaty, and Kassidy rolled her eyes at them both, and Ms. Morin began stacking chairs without being asked.

Walking out to the parking lot, Rachel read her father's text again, the one he had sent that afternoon: interested to hear how the vote goes. She stood under the streetlight holding the phone, thumb hovering, and started typing, then stopped, then started again. "Passed," she wrote. "We're taking donations. I'll tell you the rest at dinner."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: On September 17, 1925, when Kahlo was 18, a streetcar crashed into her bus, leaving injuries that caused her pain for the rest of her life.
story:
The printed reproduction of Frida Kahlo's "The Broken Column" lay on the picnic table with a sprinkler head dripping near its corner, and Brody shifted his binder to keep the ink from bleeding. Ms. Dang's assignment was due at eight the next morning: a formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism, one thousand words, no biography in the first paragraph, though after that, she had said, the life could come in if it earned its place. Brody had written four hundred words about the vertical fissure splitting the torso, about the grey desert and the white surgical corset, and then he had stopped, because he suspected he was describing rather than arguing.

Fatoumata arrived first, carrying her laptop and a bag of clementines she set down without comment, the way she always did, food appearing wherever she thought someone had forgotten to eat. Maxime came over the back fence instead of through the gate, which made the neighbours' dog start up, and he stood apologizing to the dog in a low voice until it calmed. He dropped his backpack on the table, on top of Brody's reproduction, and pulled it back immediately, smoothing the paper flat. "Sorry. Sorry. Is this the one with the nails?"

"Every inch of her skin has a nail in it," Brody said. "That's the first thing I noticed. But I can't decide if the nails are the point or if they're a distraction from the column."

Fatoumata peeled a clementine and divided it into three parts without asking whether anyone wanted any. "Then write about that. The tension between them. Ms. Dang likes when somebody admits two things are pulling against each other." She said it lightly, but Brody heard the second meaning underneath, because Fatoumata had been at his house three times this week and had seen the cardboard boxes stacked in the hallway, the ones with his father's handwriting on the sides. His parents were separating, and everyone was pretending not to mention it, and Brody had been trying to compartmentalize, to keep school in one room and home in another, but the rooms kept leaking into each other the way the sprinkler was leaking onto the grass.

"Eight tomorrow," Maxime said, checking his phone. "That's brutal. I haven't started." He tilted the reproduction toward the last of the daylight. "She looks like she's crying, but the face is calm. Why paint a calm face on a broken body?"

Brody started to answer with something about restraint, about how the flat grey sky refuses drama, and then he stopped, because a memory surfaced. In October, in the school library, he had been flipping through the big kahlo book Ms. Dang kept on the shelf behind her desk, the one with the torn dust jacket, and he had paused on a chronology in the back. September 17, 1925, the entry said. A streetcar crashed into her bus. She was eighteen. The injuries caused her pain for the rest of her life. He had read the date twice and then done the arithmetic twice, because it seemed impossible, and the impossibility was the point: she had been exactly his age, riding a bus like the one he rode to swim practice, when the whole shape of her life changed.

"She was eighteen," Brody said. "When the streetcar hit her bus. September 17, 1925. The pain never stopped after that." Maxime looked up from the painting. Fatoumata stopped typing.

"That's us," Maxime said. "That's literally how old we are."

Brody pulled the reproduction closer and looked again at the column where her spine should be, the Ionic capital at the top, the way the corset straps hold her together like packaging. "Okay, so here's my problem," he said. "Ms. Dang wants formal analysis first. But now I can't look at the composition without the accident, and I can't decide if that's me being lazy, using her life as a shortcut instead of actually looking at the paint."

Fatoumata pulled her laptop around. "So do both and be honest about the order. Look first, then admit what the looking changes into. She said the biography has to earn its place. Make it earn it. Show that the white corset is a formal choice, high contrast against the grey, before you say it's also a fact." She was talking about the essay, and she was also, Brody understood, not only talking about the essay, though neither of them would say so. Maxime had gone quiet, holding his segment of clementine without eating it, and Brody remembered that Maxime's older brother had been in a car accident two summers ago, a fact everyone at school knew and no one mentioned, and that Maxime rode his bike everywhere now, in every weather.

The light was going. Maxime turned on the porch lamp, which gave a profligate wash of yellow across the whole yard, and for a second the reproduction looked like a different painting, warmer, almost gentle, which it was not. Brody opened his notebook and wrote across the top of a fresh page: the accident is in the structure, not the story. Then, underneath: 1925. She was my age. He underlined nothing. He said, "Somebody read me my first paragraph while I fix this," and Fatoumata picked up the pages, and Brody leaned toward the lamp, his pen already moving before she found the right line.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Tennessee Williams based Laura, the fragile sister in The Glass Menagerie, on his own sister Rose.
story:
The debate tournament was scheduled to end at six, and Sara's other deadline, the one no one at this tournament knew about, was midnight. Ms. Kaminski's drama elective required a ten-minute play by Sunday, staged for the class, drawn from a moment in the playwright's own life, and Sara had two pages of a scene she did not believe in. She carried the notebook between rounds like contraband, through hallways that smelled of floor wax and vending-machine coffee, looking for a corner where nobody would ask why she wasn't highlighting evidence cards.

Her semifinal round was called for two o'clock, which gave her fifty minutes. She found a stairwell behind the auditorium and sat on the fourth step, the notebook open on her knees. The scene was about her sister, who had come home in March after leaving her first year of college, and who spent April sleeping until two in the afternoon while the rest of the household moved around her in a hush, as if noise itself could break something. Sara had written the sister fragile, mostly silent, arranging and rearranging a row of small glass animals on a windowsill, because a silent sister was easier to stage than a furious one, and the real one had been furious.

Pierre-Olivier found her there, tie loosened, holding two cans of soda. "You're hiding," he said. "You hide before every round you actually care about." He sat down one step below her and offered her a can without asking what she was writing.

"It's the play thing," Sara admitted. "For Kaminski. It's due tonight and it's about my sister and I don't know if I'm allowed to do that. Put her in it, I mean. She didn't sign up to be a character."

Pierre-Olivier popped his tab and considered this with the seriousness of someone who had once argued both sides of a privacy resolution in the same day. "People do it, though. There's a whole tradition of it." He fished in his bag, which contained, for reasons he never explained, a battered paperback of The Glass Menagerie, and flipped to the introduction. "Look. Tennessee Williams based Laura, the fragile sister in The Glass Menagerie, on his own sister Rose."

Sara took the book. She read the page twice, the way she read a card before reading it in a round, checking whether it actually said what she wanted it to say. It did. So it could be done, and it had been done, and the doing of it had produced one of the plays she'd been assigned in ninth grade. And yet. Rose had been a real person with a real life that Williams, by his own account, had bent toward shape and symbol. Laura collected glass unicorns; Rose had collected grievances and diagnoses. Was fidelity the point, or was truth? She couldn't tell if the distinction mattered or if it was the kind of distinction debaters invented to sound profound in cross-examination.

"I still don't know if I'm doing it or stealing it," she said.

"Both," said Pierre-Olivier. "Like everything."

Her phone buzzed. The semifinal was being moved up; the tab room wanted her in Room 214 in ten minutes. She closed the notebook, and the closing felt like sealing something subterranean, a thing that lived under the tournament, under the flowing water pipes and the fluorescent calm, and would have to surface eventually. On her way to 214 she passed Mahmoud in the corridor, deep in his own prep, and she felt an unexpected tenderness toward him, because he was about to argue against her with total conviction about something he'd learned yesterday. That was the skill they were all being graded on: conviction on demand. The play wanted something else. The play wanted her to sit in the ambiguity until it started to speak.

She lost the semifinal on a two-one decision. The judge said her second speech had lacked gravitas, had sounded, in his words, like she was working something out instead of closing it out, and Sara had nodded while thinking that working something out was the only honest thing her brain had done all afternoon. In the stairwell afterward, she took out the notebook and crossed out the glass animals. She wrote instead the true scene: her sister in April, standing in the kitchen at three in the morning, eating cold rice out of the pot and telling Sara, with real anger, that everyone treated her like a display case. She wrote fast, not because a deadline was chasing her but because the scene had stopped asking permission. Whether she'd show it to her sister, whether showing it would allay the guilt or double it, she left in the margin as a question without an answer.

At the bus loop at six, phone at four percent, she got a text from her sister: guess where I am. Attached was a photo of the tournament's welcome banner, taken from the parking lot. Sara stood up off the curb. Her sister was walking toward her through the rows of team vans, carrying two coffees, and the first thing she said was, "So which one of you lost, and can we get food, because I drove two hours to watch you argue and you're already done?"

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: Historian Frances Wood argued that Marco Polo may never have reached China, pointing out that his book never mentions tea, foot-binding or the Great Wall.
story:
Andrew had the essay half drafted when he found the book. He was at his desk with the lamp off, the only light coming from the monitor, and the cursor blinking at the end of a paragraph that began with confidence: In 1271, Marco Polo set out from Venice and spent seventeen years in the service of Kublai Khan. That was what the school encyclopedia said, what the first three websites said, what Mr. Hu had more or less said in class when he assigned the topic. Andrew had wanted the easy version, the one that would take ninety minutes and leave time for the game Zack kept texting him about.

Then, on the fourth website, in a footnote the color of rust, he read the sentence that undid his evening. A historian named Frances Wood had argued that Marco Polo may never have reached China at all. She had pointed out that his book never mentions tea, never mentions foot-binding, never mentions the Great Wall. Andrew sat back and stared at the words the way you stare at a door you had assumed was a wall.

He opened a video call to Edgar, who answered with his headphones half on and his whole face skeptical. "That can't be right," Edgar said. "Everyone knows he went. He's like the definition of going somewhere."

"Look it up yourself," Andrew said. He pasted the link and watched Edgar's eyes move. "It's a real historian. Frances Wood. She wrote a whole book about it."

"So the guy rode across Asia and left out tea?" Edgar began to gesticulate, one hand carving the air as if he could shape the argument into submission. "If I went to Japan I would not come home and forget to mention the toilets. That's the famous thing about Japan."

"Unless he didn't go," Andrew said. "Or went and copied other people. Or went and remembered it wrong, or somebody else wrote it down for him and cut things out."

Edgar's hand stopped midair. "Wait. So how are you going to write the essay? What's the fact?"

"That's the thing," Andrew said slowly. "There isn't one fact. There's a book that says he went, and a historian who says maybe he didn't, and she's not making it up, she's counting what isn't there. No tea. No foot-binding. No Great Wall."

"So the sources are, like, incomplete, and the answer depends on what you ask." Edgar shrugged on screen. "Sounds like every argument I've ever lost to my mom."

Andrew laughed, but after the call ended he sat for a long time with his hands off the keyboard. He thought about how the encyclopedia gave the journey dates and distances as if the past were a ledger, when really it was more like a riverbed: something metamorphic, pressed and changed by whatever lay on top of it, each layer telling you as much about who did the pressing as about the ground. He knew better than to put it that floridly in the essay. He also knew his first paragraph was now worthless.

He printed his notes and went downstairs to think somewhere other than the screen, and found his father in the kitchen holding a shoebox of photographs. This was the twist, though Andrew didn't recognize it as one at first. "Your Mr. Hu came by," his father said. "Dropped off that book you needed. He says to tell you page sixty." And then, because the shoebox was already open, his father pulled out a photograph of a harbor and told the story Andrew had heard a dozen times: the summer he'd worked a ferry out of that harbor at eighteen, the storm, the Polish cook who couldn't swim and had to be talked out of the engine room in two languages.

"You told me the cook was Turkish," Andrew said.

"Polish. Tayfun was the Turkish one, different summer." His father shuffled through the box and found nothing, and Andrew watched something careful cross his face. "Actually, the ferry was my cousin's ferry. I worked his other boat. The ferry story is his. I've been telling it so long it moved in with mine."

"Does it matter?" Andrew asked, though he already half knew the answer, and already knew it was the same question Frances Wood had asked about a Venetian merchant dead seven hundred years, in a book Andrew was going to have to cite carefully, without claiming more than she claimed.

"Probably only to the cook," his father said. He closed the box and squared it on the counter, and Andrew carried the book upstairs, where the lamp was still off and the draft waited with its confident first paragraph and its blinking cursor, and page sixty was already turned down at the corner.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Researcher Amy Edmondson described 'psychological safety' in 1999 as a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake.
story:
The garage of his grandfather's house had been converted into a workshop with a card table, two folding chairs, and a shelf of coffee tins full of screws, and it was there that David had agreed to watch Natan run through his section of their presentation one last time before regionals. Natan had built the best robot arm in their year, and he knew it, and this was the problem, because his section of the talk was eleven minutes of mumbling into a laser pointer while the slides did the work. Two teammates had already hinted at it in the group chat and then deleted the hints, and Roxane had said only, "It's fine, it's all fine," in a voice that meant it was not. David had stayed silent too. On Tuesday their teacher, Ms. Ivanova, had returned their practice rubric with a note that said the presentation lacked "clarity of oral delivery," and had added, in pencil, a single question mark next to Natan's name.

He had gone home and, more out of procrastination than research, had fallen down an internet rabbit hole that ended with a study from 1999 by a researcher named Amy Edmondson. It wasn't about robotics. It was about hospital teams, of all things, and what she found was that the best teams weren't the ones that made no mistakes, but the ones that reported more errors than everyone else, because in those teams people believed it was safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake. He'd read the phrase twice. A shared belief that it's safe to take interpersonal risks. She called it psychological safety. David had closed the laptop and thought about the group chat, about the deleted hints, about how nobody in their group of six had said the obvious thing to the one person who needed to hear it, because Natan could be thin-skinned and because it was easier to lose on Saturday than to say, out loud, on purpose, "You're not good at this part."

Now Natan clicked the clicker and the first slide bloomed against the garage wall, wrinkled by the texture of the pegboard behind it. "So, overview," Natan said. "As you can see." He turned his back to David and read bullet points to the wall.

"Natan," David said, and then, because he had promised himself he would not soften it into nothing, "stop. Turn around."

Natan turned. His face had already gone flat and ready, the face of a person bracing to be impugned. "What."

"I need to tell you something and I need you to let me finish." David's heart was going hard, which seemed absurd, since the worst that could happen here was a sulky afternoon. "Tuesday, when you asked if your part was good, I said yeah. That was a lie. Roxane lied too. Everyone lied, and it wasn't happenstance, we all chose to, because we were more scared of the conversation than of losing."

Natan sat down on the folding chair. Outside, a sprinkler started up in the neighbor's yard with its dry clicking, then the rush of water.

"And I read something this week," David went on, quieter now. "Psychological safety. It's this idea from 1999, a researcher named Amy Edmondson. It means a team's shared belief that it's safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake. We don't have it. You don't have it either, by the way. You've never once said 'I broke it' in the build log, and you've broken things, I've watched you fix them at midnight." He took a breath. "So here's my honest thing, and I'm going to be specific so it's actually usable. You say 'as you can see' six times. You face the wall. You go eleven minutes and the limit is eight. That's it. That's the whole problem. Not you. Not the arm, which is beautiful. Three things."

Natan looked at the arm on the table, its clever wrist, the weeks of solder burns on his own knuckles. He had spent the whole drive over rehearsing a defense, some speech about how speaking wasn't his job, building was, and how anyone who criticized the talking was really criticizing him. Now the speech wouldn't assemble itself. Three things. Three small, fixable, concrete things, none of which was "you are bad."

He felt peevish for about four seconds, an urge to say something cutting about David's own slide transitions, and then the urge collapsed under the weight of a worse realization: David was right, and worse, David had lied to him for weeks, politely, the way people lie to someone they've decided can't take the truth. That was the insult. Not the feedback.

"Do it again," Natan said. "The whole thing. Time me. And when I say 'as you can see,' throw this at me." He picked up a foam ball off the shelf and lobbed it to David, who caught it and grinned.

Roxane arrived twenty minutes later with her binder and her energy drink, stopped in the doorway, and stared. Natan was facing the room, shoulders down, telling the wall of tins about torque. He fumbled a sentence, restarted it, kept going. On the sixth "as you can see," the foam ball bounced off his shoulder and he laughed, actually laughed, and said the next line without it.

"Who are you," Roxane said, "and what have you done with Natan."

Natan pointed at David without turning around. "Him. Blame him. Also I'm at eight minutes even, so nobody speak until I'm done."

The sprinkler outside clicked off. David raised the foam ball and waited, and Natan, watching him in the pegboard's reflection, kept talking to the room.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues' 1993 study of violinists described 'deliberate practice': effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just logging hours.
story:
The under-twelves had scrimmaged for forty minutes, same as every Tuesday, and by the end their passing was no better than it had been in September. Austin stood at the edge of the track with his clipboard, watching a boy in a red pinnie hoof the ball straight up the middle into a wall of defenders, and felt something he couldn't yet name. He was eighteen, two years out of this league himself, and the head coach had handed him the sessions because nobody else wanted them. He'd assumed, all season, that the trouble was talent. Now, for the first time, he wondered whether the trouble was Tuesdays.

Meadow sat on the bottom row of the bleachers retying her shoes, half there to help, half there because her little brother was on the team. "You look like somebody died," she said.

"We practice all the time," Austin said. "They never get better at passing. Like, measurably never. Is that even possible?"

"Maybe they're scrimmaging wrong. Or maybe they're just twelve."

He wanted it to be the first thing. That evening he sat in the library with his phone and his clipboard and typed passing drills into the search bar, then, because that led nowhere, why practice doesn't work, which felt like a confession. An old paper came up, from 1993, a study of violinists by K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues. He read the abstract twice. What separated the best players wasn't hours logged at rehearsal. It was something the researchers called deliberate practice: effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just logging hours. He read it a third time. Scrimmage, he realized, was hours. Nothing in a scrimmage told a twelve-year-old, in the moment, that his pass had gone to nobody.

The next morning he found Luka in the cafeteria and laid the clipboard between Luka's tray and his own. Luka was the kind of person who liked to litigate everything, and Austin had learned to use that, to make him the opposing counsel. "Read that," Austin said. Luka read it, chewing.

"So you want to stop the scrimmages," Luka said. "They'll mutiny. Twelve-year-olds live for scrimmages."

"I don't want to stop them. I want to earn them. Twenty minutes of passing drills first, with a rule attached." He'd lain awake designing it. The team's weakness was concrete: they passed to where their teammate was, never to where he was going. So the drill was simple and slightly cruel. Three cones, a runner, one touch allowed. Every pass had to hit the runner's front foot, and every miss meant the runner called out the miss immediately, out loud, on the spot. Feedback before the disappointment could even fade.

"That's very rationalist of you," Luka said. "Everything reducible to a rule."

"It's not a philosophy. It's one pass."

"Fine, Counselor. But you're going to have to be the one who tells them why."

Mr. Szabó, who taught geography and had, rumor held, coached something once in Hungary or maybe just watched a lot of it, was locking the equipment shed when Austin came for the cones. Mr. Szabó looked at the diagram on the clipboard for a long moment, then at Austin, and said only, "They will hate this for two weeks." He handed over the cones and did not say anything else, which Austin found either useless or generous, depending on the hour.

They hated it for two weeks. The first Tuesday, the calls came bitterly, a small kid named for nothing but his pinnie number shouting front foot, Austin, front foot, and once a boy sat down on the track in protest and had to be negotiated with, Austin crouching beside him in the July heat, offering the deal: twenty minutes of drills, then scrimmage, then the passing rule stays on in the scrimmage too. What surprised Austin was his own reaction. He'd expected to feel like an engineer. Instead the sessions became visceral, the misses landing in his own chest as the boys trudged back to the start cone, the makes lifting something in him that he couldn't have defended in argument. Luka came to watch one evening and stood beside Meadow in the blue dusk, and afterward said, "Okay, they're not whining anymore," which from Luka was a verdict.

The fifth Tuesday, in the scrimmage, the red-pinnie boy received the ball with his back to the wall of defenders and, without looking up for more than half a second, rolled it into space ahead of a sprinting teammate, who took it in stride. Nobody on either team seemed to notice it had happened. Austin noticed. Meadow noticed him noticing, and smiled at her shoes.

The question he took home was one he hadn't expected to own. He believed in the drill now; the results were there, in front of him, in that half-second pass. And still he found himself wondering, on the walk back across the darkening track, whether the boys were getting better because of his plan or because someone was finally paying them that close, ruthless, particular attention, week after week, front foot, front foot. Maybe those were the same thing. He didn't know how you'd ever tell them apart, and he suspected you couldn't, and he kept walking anyway.

Saturday was the last match of the season. In the second half, the red-pinnie boy got the ball at midfield with two defenders closing, and Meadow's brother started his run down the left touchline, into the open, empty, perfect space.

The boy lifted his head.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane, called chemiosmosis, and won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
story:
Mya carried her biology notebook out to the irrigation pump at the edge of the hayfield because the house was too loud with her cousins and the kitchen smelled of vinegar and burnt sugar. The exam was in four days. She had written the whole pathway in blue ink, glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, and still she could not say where the ATP actually came from. She knew the mitochondria made it. She knew glucose went in. Between those two facts was a gap she could fall through.

James was already sitting on the concrete lip of the pump house, his own book open on his knees, a stalk of timothy between his teeth. "You look like the equation's wrong," he said.

"The equation's fine. It's the middle I can't hold." She sat down beside him. The metal casing of the pump was warm from the sun and smelled of engine oil and hot dust. "I can recite it. Glucose to pyruvate, pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, the cycle turns, NADH carries electrons, and then the chain pumps protons across a membrane and ATP comes out the other side. But why? Why would protons crossing a membrane make anything?"

"Ask the pump." He tipped his head at the irrigation channel behind them, where water stood high behind the sluice gate, flat and green with reflected willows. All afternoon her uncle had been complaining about the gate, how the pressure built until it hummed. When he opened it, the water ran fast enough to turn the old turbine wheel that drove the pump, and the pump pushed water up the hill to the pasture. The dam made the pressure. The pressure did the work.

Mya looked at the channel for a long time. Above them, an arboreal shadow of black walnuts moved slowly over the stubble field, and a crow called twice from somewhere inside it. "Protons," she said. "Pumped to one side. They pile up. Like water behind the gate."

"Then something lets them through," James said, "and the rush does the work."

"That's it. That's the whole thing." She was writing now, fast, drawing the membrane as two lines and the protons as a crowd of plus signs on one side. "It's not magic. It's a gradient. The cell spends the whole electron transport chain building the gradient, and then it spends the gradient making ATP." She remembered a line from the textbook's margin that she had skipped twice, a name and a date. "Mitchell. Peter Mitchell. He proposed it in 1961, that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane."

"What's it called?"

"Chemiosmosis," she said. "He won the Nobel for it in 1978. Chemistry."

James took the stalk out of his mouth. "Seventeen years between the idea and the prize."

"That's what I keep thinking." She looked at her diagram. Seventeen years was an interregnum, she thought, a gap between one king of biochemistry and the next, except nobody at the time knew who the king was. Mitchell had apparently been laughed at, that part she half-remembered too, the whole field believing in some direct chemical handoff instead. He had been right anyway. Or he had been right eventually. She wasn't sure those were the same thing, and she said so.

"So do you believe it now?" James asked. "Because it makes sense, or because it won?"

"Both. Neither." She closed the notebook, opened it again. "The dam makes sense to me. I can see the dam. But I can't see a proton, so I'm taking the gradient on faith in the same way my uncle takes the pump on faith in the county inspector." Down the hill, the sluice gate rattled and her uncle's voice rose at it, then the water broke through and the turbine wheel lurched, groaned, caught, and began to turn, and the pump shuddered against its bolts. The pipes ticked. Water climbed the hill.

"There's your ATP," James said.

She recalibrated something in her head, the whole pathway shifting from a list she had memorized to a machine she could walk around. Glucose at the top of the hill, protons behind the gate, the wheel, the pasture. She would still get the order of the carriers wrong on Tuesday, probably, and she would still write NADH where NAD+ belonged at least once. But the middle had stopped being a gap.

Her uncle came up the slope, wiping his hands on his jeans, pleased with himself and the turbine. He looked at the two of them sitting among notebooks and stalks of timothy, and at the wheel turning.

"What did you learn today?" he asked.

"That your pump runs on pressure," Mya said, "same as I do," and she snapped the notebook shut and went down to watch the water reach the pasture.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A NOT IN subquery returns no rows at all if the subquery's list contains even one NULL, a common trap when searching for missing matches.
story:
The repair shop smelled of solder and the lemon cleaner Mr. Papadopoulos sprayed when he was nervous, which today he was, because the new database he'd built to track repairs and the customers who brought them in was, in his word, lying to him. Makayla had been coming in every Tuesday and Thursday since September, officially to sweep and unofficially to sit behind the counter with his ancient laptop and learn SQL from a battered paperback he'd bought used. He'd offered her a trade: she cleaned the glass display case and answered the phone, and he let her near his data. This arrangement had seemed quaint until last week, when he'd leaned over her shoulder and asked her a real question. "I want a list of customers who never brought anything in for repair," he said. "The quiet ones. I worry about the quiet ones."

Makayla had written it in ten minutes, feeling like a wizard. Her query said, in effect, show me every customer whose ID is not in the list of customer IDs from the repairs table. It had returned four names, and Mr. Papadopoulos had been so pleased he'd printed the list and taped it inside the register, intending, he said, to call each one and ask how their phones were treating them. That was Tuesday. On Thursday she ran the same query again, unchanged, because he wanted to see the beautiful thing one more time before he called, and the screen came back empty. Not four names. Zero rows. She ran it three more times, then closed and reopened the laptop as though it were a phone she could force to restart.

"Maybe you broke it," said Andrea, who was sprawled on the stool by the register with her immunology flashcards spread across her knees, because the shop was the only place in town with both air conditioning and Mr. Papadopoulos's bottomless bowl of lemon candies. She held one up without looking. "Antigen. Do you know it or not?" Makayla said not now, and Andrea shrugged and ate the candy anyway, which was against her own flashcard rules. "You know what I think? I think the computer's being belligerent. Like my brother when you ask him to unload the dishwasher. It heard you fine. It's just deciding not to answer."

"I didn't change anything," Makayla said, mostly to herself. She scrolled through the query again, character by character, looking for a typo that wasn't there. The sentence was exactly what it had been. The data, though, the data had moved since Tuesday; she knew that much, because she'd been the one who entered a repair that afternoon for a walk-in customer, a man with a shattered tablet screen who wouldn't give his name and paid cash. She'd saved the record with the customer field blank. She'd felt a small private pride about it, about handling the exception gracefully, about not forcing a square customer into a round form. Now she opened the repairs table and looked at that row, the one with nothing where a customer ID should be, and something shifted in her chest, the way a word on a page rearranges itself into sense all at once.

Andrea watched her face change. She had known Makayla since eighth grade, long enough to recognize the particular stillness that came over her right before she either laughed or swore, and she set down her flashcards to be ready for either. What Andrea wanted, though she hadn't said it out loud to anyone, was for Mr. Papadopoulos to hire her too, because her college fund was a joke and the lemon candies were the only reliable sweetness in her week, and she'd been quietly demonstrating her reliability for a month: showing up, answering the phone politely, remembering which customer had the cracked Samsung and which had the water-damaged iPhone. She figured if she was present when Makayla figured things out, some of the credit might splatter her way. It wasn't a noble plan. She knew it wasn't. She watched Makayla's finger hover over the blank cell anyway.

"That row," Makayla said slowly. "The one with the blank customer. It's in the list now. The list the query checks against." She couldn't have explained the mechanism, not yet, not in the formal language the book used; what she had was the shape of the thing, the way you know a chord is wrong before you can name the note. "Before Tuesday, every row in that list pointed at a real customer. Now one of them points at nothing." She looked at Andrea, then at the screen. "And the whole query comes back empty. Not fewer results. Nothing at all. Zero rows because of that one blank." She laughed, finally, a short disbelieving sound. "One blank customer, and the machine just goes silent. It's not belligerent. It's worse. It's literal."

Mr. Papadopoulos came out from the back with a screwdriver in his hand and the expression of a man who had heard the word literal and knew it meant bad news. Makayla turned the laptop toward him and showed him the empty result, then the row with the blank field, and said, "Your query used not in, and when the list it checks against has even one NULL in it, it returns no rows at all. That's what happened." He lowered himself onto the stool beside her and studied the screen the way he studied a logic board before he touched it, with respect and suspicion in equal measure. "So the quiet customers," he said. "The four I wanted to call. They were there on Tuesday and gone on Thursday, and the only thing that changed is one man who wouldn't give his name." He tapped the counter twice with the screwdriver, gently, the way he tapped a case before prying it open.

"Can you fix it?" he asked, and Makayla said she thought so, that the book had a whole section on ways to find missing matches that didn't depend on that list being clean, and that she wanted to parametrize the query afterward so it couldn't be broken this way again, so the blank couldn't sneak in. Whether that would work, whether the four names would come back the same or slightly different, she couldn't promise, and she said so, and he nodded as if a promise would have disappointed him. Andrea slid off her stool and came around the counter to stand behind them both. "For the record," she said, "I was here the whole time and I answered the phone twice." Mr. Papadopoulos reached past her, took the bowl of lemon candies, and set it down between the three of them, inside the counter rather than on top of it. "Then answer it again," he said, and Makayla began to type.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: North Dakota is the only US state without voter registration; it abolished registration in 1951, and voters instead show identification at the polls.
story:
Daniel's birthday fell on the fourth of October, which meant that by the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November he would be eighteen for exactly twenty-nine days, and eligible to vote in his first general election. He had been counting on this since the summer, not because he had strong feelings about either candidate but because the act itself seemed to promise something, an entrance into a world where his opinion was counted alongside everyone else's. The registration form had been sitting on his desk for two weeks, half filled out, his signature stopped halfway through its loops.

At school on Monday, a girl named Fiona stood at the front of his civics class holding a printed sheet like it was written in another language. She had moved to the state in September from North Dakota, and Ms. Grant had told the class that anyone who turned eighteen before the election should confirm their registration. Fiona said the word "registration" the way you might say a word you had never had to use.

"I don't understand what I'm supposed to have done before," she said. "We never did any of this back home."

A boy near the window, Everett, suggested she look it up, and she sat down red-faced and spent the rest of the period typing into her phone with her thumb hovering, not pressing. Daniel watched her without meaning to. At lunch he carried his tray past his usual table and sat across from her.

"Can I see the sheet?" he said.

She slid it over. It asked for a prior address, a date of registration, a party affiliation. Fiona had written her Fargo street address in careful block letters and then stopped.

"I called the county office here," she said. "The woman told me I should have registered when I got my license, and I kept saying, registered where, and she kept saying, here, like I was being slow on purpose."

Daniel took out his phone and typed North Dakota into the search bar. The first result said it plainly, and he read it twice before he said anything, because it seemed like the kind of thing that must be wrong. North Dakota was the only state in the country without voter registration. It had abolished registration in 1951. Instead of registering, voters showed identification at the polls and that was the whole of it.

"You're not crazy," he said. "There's no such thing as registering in North Dakota. You just show up with ID."

Fiona looked at his screen, then at the half-filled sheet, then out the window at the parking lot. "So I've never been a voter anywhere," she said. "I thought I was one thing and I was the opposite."

That evening was the Sunday dinner his mother insisted on, all of them at the table whether they had anything to say or not. His father had made the pork chops with too much salt, as usual, and his younger sister was reading a book in her lap below the tablecloth, thinking nobody noticed. Daniel told the story of Fiona, mostly because it was the only interesting thing that had happened to him, and his father set down his fork.

"No registration," his father said. "Since when?"

"Since 1951. They got rid of it. It's the only state that has nothing instead of something."

His mother said it sounded like a scam, and his sister, without looking up from her book, said it sounded efficient, and the two of them began to argue about it over the pork chops while Daniel went on eating. He was thinking about the form on his desk at home, the one he had stalled on. His civics class had spent September on the franchise, and Ms. Grant had a way of talking about voting that made it sound like a sacrament, as though the ritual itself could inculcate citizenship the way his grandfather claimed the army had inculcated discipline in him. Everett, who was applying to philosophy programs, had a different line: he called voting a metaphysics problem, said it was one person trying to be two things at once, a private individual and a public integer, and that the impossibility of it was the interesting part, not a reason to skip it. Daniel had found both arguments convincing on different days, which annoyed him.

Fiona's problem had given him a third thing to think about, less abstract and harder to dismiss. She had believed she was already part of the system because she had grown up inside a version of it, and it turned out the system was fifty different systems, and her innocence about that had left her standing in a county office being talked down to by a woman who thought she was slow. If the rules could vary that much from one state to the next, then the thing Ms. Grant called the foundation of democracy was also something patched together, local, uneven. Everett would say that proved his point. Daniel wasn't sure it proved anything except that Fiona needed a form.
