He had no clean position, he decided on the walk home from school on Tuesday, and the lack of one did not feel like a failure. He believed voting mattered the way Ms. Grant said it did, and he believed it was also exactly what Everett said, a small impossible act, and he did not see why both couldn't be true at once, or why he had to resolve it before filling out a form. There were things he was uncertain about and things he was not, and the form belonged to the second kind.

That afternoon he texted Fiona and asked whether she wanted to go to the county office on Saturday, the one where the woman had talked down to her. He wrote that he was bringing his own form anyway, the one he'd stalled on, and that two half-finished registrations were better than one. She texted back a single question mark, then a thumbs up, then an address.

Saturday morning he took the form off his desk, signed it at the kitchen table in one continuous motion, and slid it into his backpack next to his wallet. At the bus stop Fiona was already there, her block-lettered Fargo address crossed out and rewritten, holding her sheet flat against the wind like a shield.

"Is your handwriting always that ugly?" she said.

"First draft," said Daniel, and the bus came.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: A lawyer who types faster than her assistant still gains by hiring him to type, because every hour she spends typing is an hour of better-paid legal work given up.
story:
The quiz was Friday, and Landon had gotten the practice question wrong twice. Mr. Paquette had written it on the board in his small, precise handwriting: Explain why two countries both gain from trade even when one country is better at producing both goods. Landon had written that the stronger country takes advantage of the weaker one, and Mr. Paquette had circled it and written "no" in red pen, which was the entire correction.

He was still staring at the board when the room emptied. Kristina packed her bag slowly, the way she did when she wanted to talk without asking to talk.

"You run that tutoring thing," she said. "Math, right? You charge for it?"

"Twenty an hour," Landon said. "Why?"

She shrugged. "My brother mows lawns. He was saying the same thing about hiring some kid to do his scheduling. He does it himself because he's faster. He's got spreadsheets." She said the word with a small affection, like the spreadsheets were a pet.

Landon walked home thinking about it, and by the time he reached his street he had started to see the shape of the problem, though not the answer. His sister handled his scheduling for five dollars a week, and she was slower than he was, messier, and she double-booked him twice in September. He had taken it back over, and since then he had spent part of every Sunday evening on emails and calendar slots, and Sunday evenings had been when he previewed the coming week's lessons for his four students.

In class the next day, Mr. Paquette put the lawyer problem on the projector. A lawyer can type faster than her assistant. Every hour she spends typing is an hour of better-paid legal work given up. Should she type? Landon read it three times. He felt something shift, small and tectonic, like a floor settling. It was not about who was faster. It was about what each hour cost.

"Both countries gain," he said aloud, before he meant to. Matthias, who sat in front of him and treated boredom as an affectation he had refined over three years, turned around.

"Congratulations," Matthias said. "That's literally the question."

"No, I mean the reason. The strong country gives up more when it makes the weak thing. So it's worth it to trade, even if it's better at everything." He was talking fast now, half to Matthias and half to the diagram forming in his head. "The lawyer is better at both jobs. She still hires the assistant, because her typing hours are expensive hours. Every hour of typing is legal work she's giving up."

Mr. Paquette had come down off the step stool he used for the projector screen and was standing by the third row, listening without commenting, which was his way of saying continue.

"That's it," Landon said. "That's the whole thing. It's called the opportunity cost. What you give up. The country gives up less of the thing it's good at when the other country does the weak thing, so both of them end up with more."

Mr. Paquette wrote "comparative advantage" on the board, underlined nothing, and said, "Friday, you'll have the numbers." Then he climbed back up the stool.

That evening Landon sat with his phone and his sister's old scheduling notebook, which she had left in the kitchen drawer with a hair tie marking March. He added up the Sunday hours: three, sometimes four, spent on emails. At twenty an hour of tutoring, and previews that made the lessons better, he had been paying himself to do clerical work. He went and knocked on her door.

"Five a week wasn't enough," he said. "Ten, and you fix the double-booking thing."

She looked up from her desk. "You yelled at me about the double-booking."

"That's why it's ten."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections.
story:
The waiting room smelled of mint and warm paper, and Nicolas had eleven minutes before the hygienist called his name, which was roughly the same amount of time he had left in his life to figure out what he was going to say tomorrow in front of Ms. Kapoor's tenth-grade health class. She had assigned him the topic herself: consent, contraception, and where to get tested for infections, delivered in five minutes, with questions after. He had agreed with the blase confidence of someone who assumed he already knew things, and had spent the past two days discovering he did not.

Aiyana sat two chairs down, disguised behind a magazine she was not reading. She had drawn the short straw on mental health and finished her slides in an afternoon, and she had appointed herself his examiner out of what he suspected was equal parts friendship and boredom. "Okay," she said, without lowering her voice, which was typical. "Someone says yes to going on the pill. Does that protect them from infections?"

"Obviously," Nicolas said. "That's the whole point of it."

Aiyana turned a page slowly, letting the silence do its work, and he felt the ground tilt under his answer. Behind the reception desk, Yohan was filing insurance forms for his summer job, and he had paused mid-stack to listen, his hand transfixed above the tray, which Nicolas found both irritating and useful, because it meant a second witness to whatever came out of his mouth next.

"I don't think it does," Yohan said. "The pill stops pregnancy. That's it."

Nicolas looked at the clock. Nine minutes. He pulled out his phone and, under the disapproving eye of a poster about flossing, called the pharmacy near his house, where he had once bought his mother's antihistamines and where the cashier knew him by sight. He asked the pharmacist, plain and direct, the way he was supposed to ask everything tomorrow: if someone has a birth control prescription, does it also protect against infections. The pharmacist said no, and Nicolas, feeling like a neophyte who had just avoided walking into a wall in front of thirty people, wrote it down on the back of his appointment card. Condoms, the pharmacist added, are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of infections. Nicolas underlined it twice.

"So say it back," Aiyana said. "The whole thing, like you're saying it to the class."

He said it: the pill prevents pregnancy but not infections; condoms are the only common method that does both; testing at the clinic downtown is free, you can walk in, and results come back in about a week. He stumbled on the consent part, which was the part he had thought would be easiest. He started with "no means no," and Aiyana stopped him and asked him what yes meant, and he sat with the question while a toddler across the room flipped the pages of a picture book, unbothered, and his mouth was dry in a way that had nothing to do with the dentist.

"Enthusiastic?" he tried. "Like, the person actually wants to, and can change their mind, and being drunk or scared doesn't count."

"And how do you know they want to?" Aiyana pressed, and he said you ask, and you listen to the answer, and you ask again if anything changes, and he thought that was maybe the only part of the whole presentation that he actually understood from the inside rather than from a website, though he could not have explained the difference out loud.

The hygienist opened the door and called his name. He stood, pockets his appointment card, and realized he still did not know what to do about the girl in the third row who always asked the question no one wanted to answer, the one about what happens if you're sixteen and already did something stupid. He had no slide for that. He had only the phone number for the clinic and the fact he had learned forty seconds ago, and the honest sentence he had decided, somewhere between the pharmacy and the flossing poster, to open with: I'm still figuring this out too, so ask me anything.

"He'll be fine," Yohan said to Aiyana as the door swung shut behind him.

"Ask me anything," Aiyana repeated, and put the magazine down at last.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the law of many jurisdictions and in consent education, consent to any intimate contact can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given.
story:
Maya would tell you she wasn't nervous, and that was true in the sense that her hands were steady and she arrived four minutes early instead of fifteen, which for her amounted to composure. The ice cream shop sat at the corner of Elm and Third, its freezers humming a torpid drone that made the whole room feel slower than the evening outside. He was already at the counter, waving, and she waved back the way you wave at someone you've only ever spoken to in the awkward acoustic of a chemistry lab.

She ordered vanilla with hot fudge. He ordered something with three mix-ins and a waffle bowl, which she decided, and then un-decided, and then decided again, was endearing. They took the booth by the window. It was a first date, technically, though neither of them had used the word; the plan had been proposed over text as "ice cream???" with the punctuation doing most of the emotional labor.

Two nights before, Tianna had come over to study for the economics final, except they had studied for roughly eleven minutes. Maya had asked, half joking, whether you could change your mind about a date after you'd already said yes. Tianna had looked up from her flashcards, one of which said stagflation in her aggressive purple ink, and said, "You know consent can be withdrawn at any time, right? Even after you already gave it. That's the whole thing." Maya had said she knew that, obviously, and they had gone back to aggregate supply, and Maya had not thought about it again until she was standing at the counter watching hot fudge pool around a scoop of vanilla.

The date was going fine. That was the honest accounting. He asked questions and listened to the answers, which put him ahead of most people Maya's age, and when the conversation stalled he didn't panic and fill the silence with noise about himself. He told a story about his little brother and a garden hose that made her laugh hard enough that the woman behind the counter glanced over. It was fine, and fine felt like a small crime, because she had wanted it to exhilarate her, and it didn't, and she kept telling herself that it still might.

Here is what Maya would not have admitted, even to Tianna, even under oath: part of her had spent the week telling a version of events in which she liked him more than she did. There had been the lab bench conversations, which she'd replayed as flirtation. There was the text with three question marks, which she'd reread as a kind of longing. She had said yes to the date under the influence of her own editing, and now she sat across from a genuinely nice boy whose waffle bowl was melting and felt her certainty drain out through the window.

They walked out into the blue half-dark, and he said his car was in the lot behind the shop. Their shoulders were close. At some point in the walk his hand found hers, and she let it, because she'd been letting things all night, small permissions granted by silence. It was warm. It wasn't bad. It just wasn't hers.

At his car he turned to face her and there was a moment where the whole next minute arranged itself visibly in the air between them, the goodnight kiss that had been implied since the three question marks. He leaned in a little, waiting, checking, which was decent of him. And Maya heard Tianna's voice with the flashcard still in her hand, saying it plain as a rule of the universe: any time, even after you said yes. She'd said yes to the date, yes to the hand, yes in small ways all evening, and she had believed, without ever articulating it, that those yeses were a contract. They weren't. She could stop. Tianna hadn't even made it sound brave, just true, the way stagflation was true, a fact you wrote on a card.

"I'd rather just say goodnight," Maya said. Her voice came out steadier than she felt, which she would later be grateful for.

He pulled back immediately. "Okay," he said. "Yeah. Goodnight." And then, because he was decent, though not the person she'd spent a week inventing, "I had a good time."

"Me too," she said, and meant it about eighty percent, which was more than she'd expected to mean anything by the end of the night. She walked home the long way, past the darkened window of the ice cream shop, her hand still warm where his had been, and she took out her phone and typed a message to Tianna and deleted it and typed a shorter one and deleted that too. Some things you got to keep undecided. At the corner of Elm and Third she stopped, looked both ways out of pure habit, and turned toward home.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parallel parking, a driver usually reverses in from alongside the car in front, turning the wheel toward the curb first and then away as the car swings into the space.
story:
The kitchen smelled of scorched butter because Alexia had left the pan on while she drew. On the notepad by the toaster she had sketched the street again: two rectangles for the parked cars, a gap between them, a third rectangle at an angle, its rear wheel kissing the curb like an apology she didn't mean. Beside her, Mikhail was buttering toast as though the toast had insulted him, which was how Mikhail did most things.

"You're turning too late," she said, rotating the notepad toward him. "You wait until you're already deep in the space, and by then the back end has nowhere to go. That's why you finish crooked every time."

"My instructor says I finish crooked because I have no spatial intelligence." He bit into the toast. "He said it in a nicer way, but that's what he meant."

Mr. Goh, who lived next door and had agreed to supervise their practice hours in his old sedan, came in through the back door without knocking, the way he always did, holding a thermos. He poured himself tea at their table as if the table were his, and in a sense it was; he'd helped Alexia's mother carry it up two flights of stairs the year they moved in, before Alexia knew his name or the fact that he'd driven delivery lorries for thirty years and had opinions about everything except the things you asked him about directly.

They had been out on the road all morning. Alexia's highway merging had gone well enough, the acceleration lane unspooling ahead of her while she watched the mirror and the oncoming traffic and the speedometer and felt, briefly, like someone juggling knives who had just discovered she could juggle. But the parking. On their street, between Mr. Goh's car and the neighbour's fence, she had tried four times and finished at an angle each time, and once she had ended up nearly two feet from the curb with the front of the car swung out like a boat refusing its dock.

"Show me what you did," Mr. Goh said now, stirring his tea. He never explained things when you were in the car. He would only say "again" or "closer" or, once, memorably, "Alexia, the curb is not lava."

She lined up three objects on the table: the toaster as the car in front, a mug as the car behind, and a small dish as the car she was driving. She pushed the dish forward until it sat alongside the toaster, even with it, close. Then she reversed it, turning it toward the gap first, so its rear swung in toward where the curb would be, and only when the rear was settling did she turn the other way, back the front end in line with the mug, and straighten. The dish slid into the space between toaster and mug, parallel, neat.

Mikhail stopped chewing. "You turn toward the curb first? Then away?"

"That's what I did," Alexia said, though she hadn't known she was going to until her hands did it. Somewhere between the fourth failed attempt on the street and this moment, her hands had figured out the argument her head kept losing. She did it again with the dish to be sure. Reverse in from alongside the car in front, wheel toward the curb first, then away as the car swings into the space. It looked obvious on the table. It had not looked obvious at half past eleven on a Tuesday with a bus bearing down.

"You've been turning away the whole time," she said to Mikhail. "From the start. So your back end never comes in toward the curb, it just goes straight back and then sideways, and the front swings out and you end up like a wedge." She demonstrated with the dish, his way, and the dish sat at the exact angle his car had sat at, and he laughed, one short pugnacious bark, because Mikhail preferred being wrong in a way that could be blamed on physics rather than on himself.

Nahla arrived then, shaking rain off her jacket, having walked from the library where she'd been studying for a different kind of test. She dropped into the fourth chair and looked at the toaster, the mug, the dish, the notepad covered in rectangles. "This is the saddest game I've ever seen," she said, and pulled the dish toward herself to examine it.

"It's not a game, it's a theory." Alexia took the dish back. "I test at the end of the month."

Nahla's older sister had failed twice, and the family had decided, in the way of families, that driving was not for their sort, a decision Nahla described with a bitterness she wore like a coat she refused to take off indoors. "You know what my father did when my sister failed the second time? He abrogated his promise to buy her the car. Just cancelled it, like a contract." She shrugged. "I keep telling myself that when I'm eighteen, I'll do it on my own, no help, no lessons. Pure will."

"That's not driving," Mikhail said. "That's asceticism."

"It's independence."

"It's the same thing, with your particular punishment attached."

They went around like this for a while, and Alexia listened with half her attention while she ran the dish through the manoeuvre again, slower now, watching the exact moment the turn had to change. Nahla wanted to do it alone as a matter of principle, refusing all help, and Mikhail wanted to blame geometry, and Mr. Goh drank his tea and offered nothing, and Alexia sat in the middle of all of it thinking that the truth was probably less dramatic than any of their positions. She had needed the hours, the failures, the neighbour's borrowed car, the notepad. She had also, in the end, needed the moment nobody could give her, when her own hands understood the thing. Both were true, and she could not have said which mattered more, and she suspected the test next month would not ask her the question in a form she could answer honestly.

The rain thickened against the window. Mr. Goh stood, rinsed his cup, and set it upside down on the rack.

"Road's empty in this weather," he said, and held out his hand for the keys.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: In a fixed-payment loan, each payment's interest is charged on the remaining balance, so early payments go more toward interest and later payments more toward principal.
story:
The loan statement had come in the mail, and Hunter's mother had left it on the keyboard of the family computer like a bill she expected him to pay. He sat down, pushed the paper aside, and opened the calculator program instead, because he had plans of his own: the used Corolla on Miller Road, four thousand dollars, and a summer of delivering parts for Mr. Vargas's shop to make the payments.

He typed the numbers his mother had written on a sticky note. Sixty payments of ninety-one dollars. He multiplied, sat back, and looked at the total. Five thousand four hundred sixty dollars. He read it twice, then leaned closer to the screen as if the number might rearrange itself.

The statement was still there, so he opened it. Six payments made. The balance had dropped from forty-one hundred to just over thirty-eight. He tapped the paper flat against the desk and did the arithmetic a third time, and the arithmetic kept saying the same thing: six payments, five hundred forty-six dollars out of his mother's account, and less than three hundred of it had touched what she owed. He pulled up a payment schedule online and ran his finger down the columns, and the pattern was there in black and white, month after month. Each payment's interest was charged on the remaining balance, so the early ones went mostly to interest and only the later ones, when the balance had finally shrunk, would go mostly to principal. He had assumed it worked the other way, that a payment was a payment. He sat with his hand on the mouse and the desk lamp buzzing faintly and the smell of his mother's burnt coffee from the kitchen.

Marco came over at eight with his backpack still on, because he'd walked straight from his shift at the pool. Hunter turned the laptop so he could see the amortization table.

"Look at payment one," Hunter said. "Of the ninety-one dollars, like seventy of it is interest. Payment fifty-eight, almost the whole thing goes to the balance."

Marco pulled a chair around and squinted. "So the bank gets its money first."

"Basically."

"Then why does anyone take these?"

Hunter hadn't answered that yet. He opened a new tab, half to avoid the question, and found a savings calculator. He typed in two hundred a month, the same money, put into an account at four percent instead, compounded. He watched the curve bend upward, slowly at first, then steeper, the mirror image of his mother's balance coming down. The bank charged interest on what was left owed and paid interest on what was saved, and time made the first shrink and the second grow.

"That's the same thing, isn't it," Marco said, reading over his shoulder. "It's an annuity either way. Just depends which side of it you're on."

Hunter nodded slowly. He had been thinking of the Corolla as a door opening, and now he was trying to historicize the feeling, to place it, to see that people had been standing on this side of the curve for as long as there had been banks. His grandfather had bought his truck with cash from a coffee can. That had seemed comical to Hunter a year ago, a Depression habit. It looked different tonight.

His mother came in from the kitchen with her cup and stood behind them. She didn't ask what they were doing; she read the screen the way she read everything, with a slightly jaundiced eye, arms folded.

"How much is left on the car?" Hunter asked her.

"Thirty-eight hundred. Why?"

"I did the math on your payments."

"And?"

"Nothing. It's just, most of what you've paid so far went to interest, not the balance."

She was quiet for a moment. The radiator ticked. "I know," she said. "The credit union woman told me, month four, when I asked why it barely moved. I sat in the parking lot for a while after."

"Why didn't you say anything?"

"Because there's nothing to say. It's the loan I could get." She rinsed her cup and set it in the rack. "You're not getting a car this summer, if that's what this is."

"I was going to ask about the Corolla."

"The Corolla's gone. Mr. Vargas's nephew bought it this morning."

Hunter looked at the tab still open on the laptop, the savings curve climbing its smooth green arc, and reached over and closed it.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: In Java, 'this.name = name' uses the keyword 'this' to mean the object's own field when a parameter has the same name.
story:
The summer before college had allotted Madison exactly one project, and she had chosen it herself with the grandiose confidence of someone who had never yet debugged anything: she would teach herself Java before orientation, so that the intro course would not eat her alive the way it had apparently eaten her cousin. She had spread her laptop, a notebook, and a paperback called Head First Java across her grandmother's kitchen table, beneath a window where the afternoon light fell across the doilies like a benediction. Her grandmother moved around her quietly, making tea, occasionally peering at the screen as though the code might turn out to be a photograph.

The chapter was about classes. She was building a small one called Student, with private fields for a name and an age, and getter methods to return them, because the book insisted that good programmers hid their fields behind methods. She typed the constructor the way the example showed, or the way she thought it showed, and then wrote a test in main: create a Student, print the name, print the age. Her grandmother set a cup of tea at her elbow and said, "Does it work yet?" and Madison said, with more certainty than she felt, "Almost."

It did not work. The output printed null for the name and 0 for the age, and Madison sat very still, the way you do when a machine contradicts you politely. She scrolled up and read the constructor again. It took a name parameter and an age parameter, and inside the brackets it said name = name and age = age, and it looked, to her eyes, perfectly symmetrical, perfectly fair. She ran it again. Null. Zero. She texted Sydnee, who had taken AP Computer Science and would know, but Sydnee was at the lake and replied only with a row of shrugging emojis and the words "idk maybe ur computer is haunted."

"You look like your grandfather when the truck wouldn't start," her grandmother said, drying a saucer. "He'd stare at the engine as if it would feel guilty."

"It's not the computer's fault," Madison said. "That's the worst part. It's doing exactly what I told it." She pulled the notebook closer and wrote the constructor out by hand, slow as a schoolchild, name = name, and stared at it until the words desiccated into marks on the page, meaningless and dry. There was a version of this where she quit. She could picture it: the laptop closed, the paperback returned to the library, September arriving anyway, the intro course eating her alive on schedule. She had promised herself she was not that version of herself, though she noticed the promise was easier to make in June.

The doorbell rang, and it was Ms. Holloway from next door, returning a casserole dish and staying, as she always did, for the perimeter of one conversation. She had taught math at the high school for thirty years, retired now, and she leaned over Madison's shoulder with the dish under her arm like a shield. "Null," she read aloud. "When I got null in my gradebook, it meant I'd never entered the grade at all. Something was never set."

"That's it," Madison said slowly. "It was never set. But I set it, I wrote name equals name." She looked at the line, and then, for no reason she could name, she looked at the chapter heading a few pages back, where a word she had skimmed past sat waiting in bold. "Wait," she said, out loud, to Ms. Holloway, to her grandmother, to the kitchen. "There's this word. This. In Java, 'this' means the object's own field when the parameter has the same name." She said it twice in her head. The parameter was name. The field was also name. She had written name = name and the two names had simply passed each other by, assigning the parameter to itself, the field left untouched at null.

She typed this.name = name, ran it, and the console printed the actual name and the actual age, plain as bread. She laughed, a short startled bark, and her grandmother said, "Is that good?" and Madison said, "It's so good," and Ms. Holloway said, "Thirty years of teaching and the bugs were always the same. Something that looks like it's connecting two things and isn't."

Vera called at dusk, from her own porch across town, and Madison told the whole story with the window open and the moths beginning. "So you spent three hours on one word?" Vera said.

"Five letters," Madison said. "And I'm going to spend the fall being grateful for every one of them." She was half joking, but not entirely. She had walked into the afternoon believing that writing code meant having grand ideas, and she was walking out of it believing something less grandiose and more useful, though she could not yet say what: that the machine would obey her exactly, and that her enemy was not the language but her own assumption that looking right and being right were the same thing. Whether she could actually hold both of those in her head at once, whether she could be ambitious and humble in the same keystroke, was not something one afternoon could settle, and she knew it.

She stayed at the table after dark with the kitchen lamp on, building the getter methods, testing each one, watching the values come back. Her grandmother came through in her slippers to say goodnight, paused behind her chair, and read the screen over her shoulder. "this.name," she said, tasting it. "Like pointing at yourself."

"Exactly like that," Madison said, and typed the next line.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces.
story:
Austin crouched beside the cooler, lifting packets of chicken thighs one at a time and laying them on the folding table like evidence in a trial he hadn't agreed to preside over. His parents had driven his sister to the nearest town for a forgotten inhaler, which left him, at eighteen and technically an adult, in charge of dinner for six at the campsite. His grandmother's voice sat in his head the way it always did when raw chicken appeared: rinse it first, always rinse it, that was the family maxim, spoken with the certainty of someone who had survived two wars and one divorce. So he turned on the spigot at the washing station, held the first thigh under the stream, and watched the water splash off the pale skin and spatter the basin, the table edge, his sleeve.

"Whoa, whoa." Matteo came around the tent with a bag of foil in one hand and the expression of a man witnessing a crime. "Dude. You wash chicken?"

"My grandma washed chicken," Austin said. "My mom washes chicken. Everybody washes chicken."

"I don't wash chicken," said Alia, who had followed Matteo out and was now standing with her arms crossed in a way that suggested she had been waiting years for this exact moment. "The CDC says don't. Washing raw chicken splashes bacteria all over the sink and the surfaces around it. You're basically pressure-washing germs onto everything we're about to eat off of."

Austin looked at the thigh in his hand, then at the spattered basin, then at the sleeve he had been planning to wipe his forehead with later. He held very still, the way a person does when they realize they have been confidently wrong in front of witnesses. "That can't be right. People have washed chicken forever."

"People have done lots of things forever," Alia said. "Look it up if you don't believe me."

He looked it up, thumbing his phone with one hand while the other held the chicken at arm's length, as though the thigh itself had opinions. The page confirmed it, plainly, in the flat prose of an agency with no interest in his grandmother's honor: the CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces. He read it twice. Somewhere in his chest, two loyalties that had never had to meet before were now standing in the same room, staring at each other.

"That's genuinely disgusting, by the way," Matteo said, peering at the washing station. "You splashed the whole thing."

"Okay, I can fix this." Austin set the chicken down on a clean plate, found the bottle of sanitizer wipes, and began wiping the basin, the table edge, the folding handle of the spigot, moving with the focused energy of someone who would rather scrub than think. But the thinking happened anyway. His grandmother had learned to wash chicken from her mother, in a kitchen where the meat came from a market with sawdust on the floor, and maybe rinsing had made sense then, or maybe it had never made sense and had simply been passed down like a recipe. The CDC wasn't insulting her; it was just answering a different question than she had ever been asked. Both of them wanted the same thing, he decided, which was that nobody get sick, and if the newer answer got that result better, then following it wasn't a betrayal. It was just a revision. Though, he had to admit to himself, wiping down a campsite washing station, there was a smaller question he still couldn't settle: whether his grandmother would laugh at this story at Thanksgiving or go quiet and hurt. He genuinely did not know.

"Does this mean I'm the most hygienic person in your family now?" Alia asked. "Because I want that on a shirt."

"You're the most hygienic person in your own family," Austin said. "You brought hand sanitizer to a campsite where we are going to eat with sticks."

"Tongs," Matteo said. "We have tongs. I carried them for a mile in my backpack like a hero, and this is the thanks I get."

By the time the fire had settled to a torpid glow of coals, Austin had the thighs seasoned and laid over the grate, and the three of them sat on the cooler and a log, watching fat drip and hiss. The smell came up off the chicken slowly, then all at once, smoke and pepper and something almost sweet. Ms. Rao, the retired teacher who kept the neighboring site and had drifted over at the first mention of food, was telling them about a student who had once turned in an essay arguing that all camping should be illegal. Austin mostly listened. When the meat was done he tested a thigh the way his father did, tearing it at the joint to see the interior, white and clean, steam extruding from the fibers in thin threads, and for a second the sight of that steam made something in him settle.

His parents' car crunched onto the gravel just as he was plating, his sister already complaining about the long drive, and his mother came over and looked at the table and said, "You didn't rinse the chicken?"

"No," Austin said, and handed her a plate. "I'll tell you about it while we eat."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A getter that returns a reference to a private mutable object, such as a list, lets outside code change it, so programmers often return a copy instead.
story:
The computer lab smelled of warm dust and floor wax, and the radiator under the window ticked the way it always did in November, as though the building were counting down to something. Leo sat two rows from the back with his program open on both monitors, the left showing his Player class, the right showing the test file Warren had written without asking. On the left screen, the fields were tidy and private: name, score, and a list called badges, because Mr. Silva had been firm about that all semester. Private fields. Getter methods. Nothing touches the inside of a class from the outside.

"You're going to like this," Warren said, sliding into the chair beside him with the confidence of someone who had already decided. He had a black marker smudge on his wrist from the whiteboard, and his sneakers were untied in the way that made Mr. Silva wince every time he passed. "I wrote a test that checks the badges. Watch. I call the getter, I clear what it gives me, then I ask the size."

"Clear it?" Leo said. "Why would you clear it?"

"Because it's a test. You break things in tests. That's the whole point." Warren was already reaching for Leo's keyboard, and Leo demurred, pulling the keyboard toward himself, not unkindly, just enough that Warren laughed and put his hands up in surrender. "Fine, you drive. But run it."

Leo ran it. The test printed a size of zero where it should have printed three, and for a moment he sat very still, because the badges were gone. Not gone in the file, he could see them right there in the constructor, gold, silver, bronze, added one by one in the first three lines. Gone in the running program, in the thing itself. Warren's class had reached in and emptied the list, and the list was private, and those two facts sat side by side in Leo's head without agreeing.

"That's a fail," Warren said, and there was something careful in his voice, the way people get careful when they suspect they have broken something that mattered to someone. "Sorry, I didn't think it would actually do anything. The field's private."

"It is private," Leo said slowly. "But the getter gives back the real list. Not the name of it. The actual thing." He turned to the right monitor and scrolled up through Warren's test, three short lines, and read them again as if the words might rearrange themselves. getBadges, then clear, then getBadges again, then size. It was all so plain. The getter handed out a reference to the private list, and outside code could change it through that, privacy and all, which meant his design had a hole shaped exactly like his own good intentions.

Across the room, Santino was elbow-deep in a bracket error, muttering to himself, and Mr. Silva moved between the rows the way he did, hands behind his back, pausing at screens without comment. When he stopped behind them, Leo did the thing he had taught himself to do with Mr. Silva, which was to state the problem rather than ask for the answer. "My getter returns the list itself," Leo said. "So the private field can still be changed from another class."

Mr. Silva looked at the screen for a moment longer than seemed necessary, then said only, "What do people often do about that?" and moved on toward Santino, which was so like him that Warren exhaled half a laugh. Leo stared at the word private and thought about his mother's recipe box, the one she lent to the neighbours last spring, and how it had come back with a card missing and a new one in her sister's handwriting. Lending the box was not the same as lending a copy of the cards. That was not a cerebral leap, it was a kitchen table one, and it arrived with the smell of Sunday rice, which was the strange way his mind worked when it worked at all.

He changed the getter to build a new list, copy the badges into it, and return that instead. Then he sat with his hands off the keyboard, because Warren's test would now clear the copy and the real list would keep its three badges, and if that was right it was right for a reason he could defend, and if it was wrong he wanted to watch it be wrong in front of him rather than hope it was right. He ran it. Size three. He ran it again. Size three.

"Okay," Warren said, and pushed back in his chair, and looked at Leo with an expression that had shifted somewhere in the last ten minutes from apology to something more like respect, though he would never have named it. "So the fix is you give out a copy. That's it?"

"That's it for today," Leo said. "Whether it's the right habit for everything, I don't know yet." It was an honest answer and it cost him something to make it, because part of him wanted to declare the problem solved and be finished. Instead he saved the file twice, once in the lab folder and once to his drive, which was his small private ritual of not trusting any single place to hold anything, and turned to see Santino waving them over, his bracket error still bleeding red across the screen.

"Five minutes of your life," Santino said, "and I'll owe you recompense. Snack machine, anything under two dollars."

Warren was already standing. Leo looked at his own screen one more time, at the getter with its quiet new copy, then followed them across the room. "Make it three dollars," he said. "I cleared a whole list for you today."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: A 2001 review titled 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good', led by Roy Baumeister, found that negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size.
story:
Chase sat on the floor of Ali's kitchen with his laptop balanced on a stack of wrestling magazines, watching the clip for the eleventh time. In it, Lara took a touch, cut inside, and shot the ball into the side netting from twelve yards. Ali's mother had left a plate of sliced apples on the counter, and they had gone brown and desiccated while he watched, which was roughly how long he had been putting this off. The feedback was due at nine, when Coach posted the team thread, and it was already 8:31.

"Are you going to write something or just glare at it?" Ali asked. She was at the table with a chemistry textbook open to a page about entropy, which she claimed explained the state of her bedroom, and she didn't look up when she said it.

"I already wrote something. That's the problem." He turned the laptop so she could see the message he'd sent Lara two days ago, after the scrimmage. It said her positioning was excellent, her first touch was the best on the team, her passing was sharp, she read the game well, and her left foot needed work when she shot under pressure. Five good things and one bad thing. He'd been careful. He'd even counted.

"And?" Ali said.

"She replied with one line. 'So you think I can't finish.' That's it. She's been flat at practice since. Cold at me in the hallway." He closed the laptop, opened it again. "I told her five good things. One bad thing. She kept the bad one."

Ali finally looked up. "So say it differently."

"It's not the wording. It's the math of it. There's something wrong with the math." He got up and paced the length of the kitchen, which took four steps. On the counter beside the dead apples lay a photocopied article that Ms. Mokoena, who tutored Ali's younger brother on Tuesdays, had left behind. The title was underlined twice in her green pen: "Bad Is Stronger Than Good," a review led by a psychologist named Roy Baumeister. Chase picked it up because he had nothing left to try and because the title sounded like his whole week.

He read the first page standing. Then he read it again. "Listen," he said. "In 2001, this guy Baumeister reviewed the research, and it says bad stuff, bad events, bad remarks, hit people harder than good stuff of the same size. Same size. So it doesn't matter that I said five nice things. The one bad thing was heavier." He set the page down. "It's not that she's sensitive. It's that anybody would do this. I would do this."

"Then what's the fix?" Ali said. "You can't just never tell her about the left foot."

"That's the part I don't know." He checked the clock: 8:44. "The article says what's true. It doesn't say what to do about it. I think maybe the criticism can't just be smaller. It has to be more specific. 'Left foot under pressure' isn't a thing she can hold. It just sits there being bad. But 'when the defender closes on your left, pull the ball back and switch feet, like in the second half when it worked' is a thing she can do. That's not a compliment. It's still the same fact. It's just shaped like help instead of like a verdict."

Ali tapped her pencil against the textbook. "Or she wants it blunt. Some people want it blunt."

"Some people say they do and then don't. I don't know which she is. I'm going to guess specific-and-kind, and if I'm wrong I'll find out tomorrow." He typed, deleted, typed. At 8:52 he sent it: her cut in the clip was the best on the team, her touch had set the whole move up, and if she pulled the ball back and switched feet when the defender closed from her left, the same shot goes in; she'd already done it once in the second half, he'd seen it. He put the phone face down on the counter and exhaled.

The reply came at 9:06. "Oh. Okay. That one I can do." Then a second message, arriving while Ali was grinning at him over the entropy homework: "Also, your throw-ins drift to the middle every time and the other team knows it. You never noticed? Fix that before Saturday."

Chase read it twice and put the phone in his pocket.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
The phone repair shop smelled of solder and lemon cleaner, and William sat on a stool behind the counter watching Mr. Mwangi pry the back off a water-damaged tablet. He had taken the summer job to learn something practical, how screens were fused, how batteries swelled, but the repair bench had turned out to be a quieter school than he expected.

"Your sister came by," Mr. Mwangi said without looking up. "She left this." He slid a phone across the counter, its screen cracked into a spiderweb. On the lock screen, visible through the fractures, was a notification from the group chat: Keeley had sent the video again, tagged with William's name.

The video showed a warehouse fire, and the caption claimed it had happened that morning in their city, set by a group of striking workers. William had shared it three weeks ago without watching it twice. Tyler's father worked at that warehouse, or one like it, and within a day the story had gone around the whole grade. By the weekend, Tyler wasn't speaking to him, and someone had printed stills from the video and taped them inside Tyler's locker with words William wouldn't repeat. The fire, it turned out, was real, but it had happened four years earlier, in another country, with a different cause entirely. William had learned this from Mr. Mwangi, the afternoon he came in to buy a charging cable and stayed to confess.

"You want to fix this one?" Mr. Mwangi asked, nodding at the cracked phone. He meant the phone. William picked it up anyway and turned it over, as if the truth were a ribbon cable that had simply come loose.

Keeley came in at five, jangling the bell, holding her own phone like an accusation. "Everyone's saying you told the principal it was me who started the rumor," she said. "I sent the video, but you shared it. You added the part about the strike."

William had done exactly that. He had written a caption, his own small invention, because it made the video feel like news. He set the phone down. "I didn't say anything to the principal. I want to show you something first." He woke the shop's loaner tablet and opened an image search, dragging in a frozen frame from the fire. The results assembled themselves slowly: the same warehouse, the same smoke plume, dated years before, attributed to an electrical fault. He had done this search a dozen times since that afternoon, partly to punish himself, partly because he couldn't quite believe how easy it had been, how the whole machinery of checking had been sitting there all along while he hit share.

"Mr. Mwangi calls it the SIFT method," William said. "Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to their original context. Some educator named Mike Caulfield came up with it." He'd found the name on a library page, printed it, and folded it into his wallet like a receipt for a debt.

Keeley looked at the screen, then at him. "So you're the expert now? You stigmatized Tyler's dad's whole union in one caption, and now you're the one lecturing me about sources?"

"I'm not lecturing." He paused. "I'm saying I did it wrong and I'm trying to learn to do it right, and I don't know yet whether that's enough." He thought of his history teacher, who had once said that historiography was the study not of what happened but of how people wrote it down, and William had thought the word was useless and abstract until he watched a four-year-old fire become a strike become a riot become a headline, each teller adding a floor to the building.

Keeley sat down on the second stool, which she had never done before. "It was facetious at first, you know. My caption. I thought it was funny." She rubbed her thumb along the tablet's edge. "It stopped being funny around Thursday."

Mr. Mwangi reassembled the tablet, pressed the power button, and held his breath out of habit. The screen lit. He set it between the two of them, the search results still glowing, and said nothing at all, just slid the spudger across the counter toward William's hand.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, families light small oil lamps called diyas in homes and temples to symbolize light overcoming darkness.
story:
Maya's mother wanted the diyas finished before the Chaudhris arrived at seven, which gave her forty minutes to fill small clay bowls with oil, press in cotton wicks, and set them in rows along the front steps, the windowsills, and the ledge of the garden wall. Her grandmother, visiting from Jaipur for the festival, supervised from a kitchen chair pulled halfway into the hallway, calling out corrections in Hindi whenever a lamp drifted out of line. Diwali, she said, was celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, and the lamps meant the same thing in every one of those houses: light overcoming darkness. Maya had heard this every year of her life, and every year it landed differently, the way a word repeated until it breaks open.

This year it landed on the morning's argument. She had spent two hours before lunch drafting an email to the admissions office asking to switch her declared major from biology to undecided, and her father had spent forty-five minutes after lunch explaining, gently and then less gently, why undecided was a waste of a semester's tuition. He taught high school chemistry; he believed in sequences. Pre-med prerequisites in the first fall, shadowing in the spring, the MCAT by junior year. She believed in sequences too, or she had, right up until the epidemiology unit in her spring elective, when the maps of outbreak clusters had made her feel something she couldn't name while the anatomy diagrams never had.

"How many along the wall?" her grandmother asked, craning to see through the doorway.

"Fourteen," Maya called back. "Fifteen if I space them out."

"Twenty. It should look like a river."

Leana arrived at six-thirty with a tin of her mother's gulab jamun and a flyer for a party at Jagger's house, two streets over, starting at nine. She stood on the front path with her thumbs hooked in her jacket pockets, watching Maya work, and after a while she crouched and began lifting the lamps Maya had already placed, turning each one so the wick faced the same direction.

"You're going to the party after," Maya said. Not a question.

"Come for an hour. Jagger asked if you were." Leana set down a diya with unnecessary care. "You leave in three weeks. What's the argument for sitting here all night with your grandmother's friends?"

Maya didn't have an answer ready, which annoyed her. She had spent the whole spring learning to build arguments, and the habit had begun to feel like a liability. Leana's case was sound: she was eighteen, the party was close, her parents would say yes if she asked. Her father's case was sound too, in its way, the sequence of it, the rails already laid. And underneath both of them was a third thing, harder to say out loud, which was that she genuinely did not know which she wanted, and the not-knowing felt less like weakness lately and more like information. Maybe the wishy-washy feeling in her chest was a signal, the way an outbreak cluster was a signal, a pattern waiting to be read rather than a fault to be corrected.

The Chaudhris' car pulled up at seven sharp, and the last twenty lamps still needed lighting. Her grandmother insisted this be done with a single match passed down the row, each wick leaning to the next, though Maya noticed that in practice the flames caught unevenly and someone always had to double back. That was the part nobody said in the retelling. The version her grandmother told was a straight line of light; the version Maya could see from the porch was a staggered one, half the row lit, the other half catching in its own time, and both versions were true at once, which seemed worth noticing rather than resolving.

At the door, greeting the Chaudhris, asking after their son's new job in Toronto, passing plates of mithai, Maya caught herself observing her own hands performing each courtesy and thought, with a small inward jolt, that she was already practicing the acclimating she would need in a dorm in three weeks. Everything was rehearsal, apparently, including this.

She lit lamps until her fingers smelled of smoke and oil. Through the window she could see her father laughing at something Mr. Chaudhri had said, his argument from lunch apparently dissolved, and Leana's text sat unanswered in her pocket, the party address glowing whenever she checked it. Around ten her grandmother fell asleep in the armchair, the news murmuring in Hindi, and Maya stood alone on the front step in her good kurta, looking down the street. Jagger's block glowed faintly, ordinary porch lights and a knot of cars. Behind her, forty small flames trembled along the wall in the wind, going out and being relit, going out and being relit.

She sat down on the step and pulled out her phone. "Saving you a gulab jamun," she typed to Leana, "and I'll decide by eleven." Then she set the phone face-down beside her, took the box of matches from her pocket, and struck one.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle, and he published it in the journal Enzymologia instead.
story:
Tristan had dragged the whiteboard out to the backyard because inside the house his rejection letter was still sitting on the kitchen table, and he could not look at it and think at the same time. The letter was two sentences long. The regional science fair committee regretted to inform him that his entry, "A Working Map of Cellular Respiration," had not been selected for the final round. He had drawn the whole thing himself, glucose splitting in the cytoplasm, the shuttle across the membrane, the slow turning of the cycle in the mitochondria where the actual payoff happened, and someone had read it and said no in two sentences.

Maria arrived first, cutting through the back hedge the way she always did, and Charles-Antoine came ten minutes later with his bike still rolling when he dropped it in the grass. They had agreed to study for the biology exam together, though Tristan suspected they had also come because of the letter. Maria picked up a dry-erase marker and uncapped it without asking.

"So teach it," she said. "You're the one who spent four months on this."

He started where the textbook started, with glucose, six carbons, getting split in half in the cytoplasm like a loaf broken for two guests. Then the pieces got shuttled inside, and in the mitochondria they entered the cycle, losing carbons, giving up electrons, so that at the end a spinning machinery in the inner membrane could pack energy into ATP. Charles-Antoine lay back on the picnic blanket and watched a wasp ferment whatever had gone bad in the compost bin against the fence. "That's what happens without oxygen," Tristan said, pointing at the bin. "It ferments. Sour, inefficient, but alive."

"You sound like a textbook with feelings," Charles-Antoine said, but he sat up.

The problem was that Tristan's science fair board had put the cycle at the centre, drawn as a wheel with eight spokes, and the judges' form had one comment in handwriting he couldn't read. He had made it beautiful and he had made it correct and it had still been refused, and for three days he had let that ferment inside him too, until he was less a student and more something belligerent, snapping at his mother about dishes, kicking the recycling bin when it wouldn't close.

Mr. Tse leaned over the fence then, watering can in hand, the way he did when he heard voices. He was retired, they knew that much, and he grew tomatoes with a seriousness that suggested he had once applied it elsewhere. Tristan, tired of being handled gently, told him the whole thing, the four months, the wheel, the two-sentence letter.

"Rejected," Mr. Tse repeated. He watered a staked plant with great attention while he thought. "Hans Krebs worked out that same cycle of yours, the citric acid cycle. In 1937 he wrote it up and sent it to the journal Nature, and Nature rejected his paper. He published it in a journal called Enzymologia instead." He set the can down. "You'd know his name if you've read your textbook's fine print. It's the Krebs cycle." Then he picked up a fallen tomato stake and went back to his own yard, as though he had only been reporting the weather.

Nobody said anything for a moment. Maria wrote the fact on the whiteboard's corner in small letters, under where she had been tracing the electron path, and Tristan looked at the two things side by side: the cycle he had drawn, and the sentence about the man who had drawn it first and been told no. He was not sure what he was allowed to conclude. Nature was not the science fair committee, 1937 was not now, and a paper that later earned a Nobel Prize had still been turned away once, which meant either that rejection meant very little or that it meant something and people survived it anyway. Both of those could be true. He held them together the way you hold two magnifying glasses, one in each hand, not sure which one would bring the page into focus.

Charles-Antoine broke the silence. "So the greatest discovery in your whole unit couldn't get published the first time, and your board couldn't get past a folding table in a school gym. I'm not saying they're the same."

"They're not the same," Tristan said.

"They're not the same," Charles-Antoine agreed.

Maria tossed him the marker. "Fine. Then stop staring at the fence and finish the wheel. Exam's Thursday and some of us don't have a rejection letter to mope about." Tristan caught it, wiped the corner of the board clean with his sleeve, and drew the first arrow, from glucose, in a line that curved inward toward the mitochondria like a road he already knew.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A statistically significant result can still be a tiny effect: with a very large sample, even a difference too small to matter in practice can pass the significance test.
story:
The photocopied articles had been waiting in Antoine's bag since Monday, and by Thursday night they had migrated to the floor beside his bed, where he stepped on them getting up for water. He was supposed to compare them, two studies asking the same question, whether countries with stricter religious institutions report harsher public attitudes toward depression. One was written by a team at a large university, the other by a single researcher whose prose was so incisive it made him suspicious; sentences that clean, he thought, had to be hiding something.

He brought both articles to school in the morning and spread them across a table in the library during free period. Esme slid into the chair opposite him with her own work, glanced at his pages, and asked what he was doing. He showed her the first study's headline claim, that religiosity of a nation's institutions predicted more negative attitudes toward mental illness, and that the difference was significant. He said the word the way the article said it, like a door closing.

"Significant how?" Esme asked. She was eating an apple and did not look up from her notes.

Antoine went back to the results table and found the two numbers, the average attitude score in more secular countries and the average in more religious ones, and copied them into the margin. Then he sat looking at what he had written, because the gap between them was smaller than the gap between anything. On the study's own scale, the difference came out to less than a tenth of a point. The survey had covered a quarter of a million people across sixty countries, and with a sample that enormous, he realized, even a difference too small to matter in practice could pass the significance test. He read the sentence three more times to be sure he had the direction right, that the test said the difference existed, not that it was big.

"Drayden," he called across the library, quietly enough not to be shushed. Drayden came over, munching whatever he had taken from the vending machine, and Antoine showed him the two averages. "If I told you people in theocratic countries scored, what, a tenth of a point lower, would you say that matters?"

"On that scale? That's nothing," Drayden said. "Nobody feels a tenth of a point."

"But it's significant," Antoine said. "Statistically significant. The test says the difference is real. It just doesn't say it's big." Saying it out loud, he felt the two halves of the sentence lock together, and also felt where they didn't lock: real and small at once, and no clean way to decide when small became too small.

The second article complicated it further. Its author had interviewed eighty people in three countries and argued that the stigmatizing attitudes came not from religion itself but from how local clerics chose to talk about illness, so that two towns with identical institutions could differ enormously. Her sample was tiny and she never claimed significance at all. Antoine had dismissed her on Tuesday for being unrigorous, and now he kept flipping between the two papers, the huge study that found a real sliver and the small one that found a whole landscape it couldn't measure.

He drafted a paragraph after lunch, in Ms. Müller's empty classroom during her office hour, and she read it while he watched. She underlined one sentence and turned the page back to him. "Which article do you think got it closer to the truth?" she asked.

"I don't know yet," Antoine said. "The big one found something that's probably real. But it might be too small to care about, and the small one might be describing the thing that actually matters, and has no way to prove it." He looked at his own sentence, the one she had underlined, which claimed the large study had demonstrated a meaningful effect, and crossed out the word meaningful. "I want to write that one is right," he said. "It would be easier."

Ms. Müller smiled at that and handed back the draft. Esme appeared in the doorway with the last of her apple, holding it up like a small trophy, and asked if he had figured out which paper to trust.

"Neither," Antoine said, and picked up his pen.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back in student housing found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends.
story:
The movers took four hours, and by the end of it Olivier's mother was arguing with the driver about the television while Olivier stood in his new room holding a shoebox of things he had refused to let them pack. The box held a broken watch, a river stone, and eleven folded notes from his friends back in Harrowgate, most of them variations on "text me every day," which he already knew he would not do. School started in six days. He had looked up the enrollment number, nine hundred and forty, and done the arithmetic without meaning to: if friendship were distributed evenly, his chances were excellent; he knew enough by sixteen to know it was not distributed evenly.

On the first day he was assigned locker 214 in the west corridor, at the far end, past the water fountain that no one used because it made a sound like a dying animal. He ate lunch at a table for two near the windows and watched the stairwell by the cafeteria, where a knot of students gathered and re-formed every fifty minutes like water finding the same drain. He recognized two of them from his English class, Eamon and a girl named Kacey, and he recognized something else too, which was that nobody in the knot had sought it out. They had simply been deposited there by the architecture.

That was not yet a thought he could defend. It was closer to a suspicion, and he held it the way he held most suspicions, privately and with a certain asceticism, refusing to let himself hope until he had evidence. In the public library on Ashbury Road he found a sociology section wedged between careers and large print, and pulled down a textbook with a cracked spine. In a chapter on group formation he read about a 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back, done in student housing, which found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends. He read the sentence three times, then copied it onto his hand because he had no paper.

The study did not say people chose their friends, or that friendship was luck. It said something narrower and stranger: that distance did most of the work before personality got a chance to. He sat with that. It offended a belief he hadn't known he held, the belief that the friends you made were the friends you deserved. His father had said a version of it at dinner before they moved: "You'll find your people, Olivier. The right ones always find each other." Olivier had equivocated at the time, saying "probably" into his potatoes, because he did not want to argue and because he suspected it was false.

He decided to test it, which felt scientific and also slightly dishonest, like counting cards. On Wednesday he took his lunch to the bench six feet from the cafeteria stairwell and ate without looking at anyone. Nobody spoke to him. On Thursday he moved to the bench directly beside the stairwell, close enough that students had to angle their bags around his knees. By the end of lunch, Eamon had asked him whether the bench was taken, sat down without waiting for the answer, and complained for four minutes about a substitute in geography. On Friday, Kacey arrived carrying a Rubik's cube she could not solve, set it on the bench between them, and said, "Someone in this building has to know how."

He did not know how. He picked it up anyway and turned one face, and she watched him the way people watch a magician to catch the trick. "You're the guy from Harrowgate," Eamon said. "Olivier, right? You corrected Mr. Reddy about the Mississippi." Mr. Reddy taught history and had misstated the length of the river, and Olivier had raised his hand, and he had regretted it for two days. "It was in the textbook," he said now, and Kacey said, "He still hates you," and Eamon said, "No, he loves him, he's going to make him do the debate," and it turned out that Mr. Reddy had already posted the debate teams on the door of room 118, and Olivier was on one, paired with Eamon, arguing against the abolition of the electoral college, a position he did not hold.

They met Sunday at the library on Ashbury, in the sociology section by accident because the other tables were full. Kacey was there too, ostensibly for the cube, which Olivier had learned to solve from a video and could now do in under three minutes, though not smoothly, his fingers stuttering on the last algorithm. Eamon spread the debate notes across a table and said, "Give me one argument, just one, that isn't garbage." Olivier told them about the study instead. He said it plainly: in 1950, Festinger, Schachter and Back looked at student housing and found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends.

"That's bleak," Kacey said.

"It's not," Olivier said, and then stopped, because he was not sure it wasn't. "It's just how it starts. It doesn't say how it keeps going."

Eamon leaned back. "So we're only friends because of the stairwell."

"We're only talking because of the stairwell," Olivier said. "I don't know what we are."

Kacey took the cube back and scrambled it, her thumbs working fast, and set it on the shelf beside Festinger's name in the index, so that both of them were in view at once, the puzzle and the explanation, neither one adequate to the other. "Solve it again," she said, and pushed it toward him, and he reached for it before he had decided to.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In Jewish law, the principle of pikuach nefesh holds that saving a human life overrides almost every other commandment, including the rules of the Sabbath.
story:
Juliette spread the photocopies across the kitchen table until they overlapped like shingles, three translations of Exodus and a commentary she'd printed at the library because the household printer had been out of ink since March. The debate was in four days. The resolution said the ancient rules of the Sabbath could not survive modern life, and she had drawn the side defending them, which was a problem, because until Tuesday she had never given the Sabbath a single thought.

Tommy arrived first, dropping his backpack by the fridge and sliding a granola bar across the table to her like a bribe. "Jaeden's coming," he said. "He says he found something that destroys your whole case." He said it cheerfully, the way he announced most catastrophes.

"What," Juliette said, not looking up.

He wouldn't tell her. He peeled the wrapper off the granola bar and read upside down the passage she'd underlined twice, the one about kindling no fire, and asked why she'd marked it. "Because it's strict," she said. "A rule you can break for nothing isn't a rule worth debating." She liked that sentence and wrote it in the margin so she'd remember it later, which was how she worked, exhuming her own best lines from the wreckage of conversation.

Jaeden came through the back door without knocking, holding his phone like a serving tray. "Okay," he said. "Hypothetical. Saturday, Sabbath, your grandmother's neighbor collapses. No ambulance for an hour, roads are a mess, but your uncle has a car. Is he allowed to drive?"

"Of course he's allowed."

"It's the Sabbath," Jaeden said. "Your side says the rule applies. No driving, no fire, no work. So either your uncle sits there with his keys on the counter, or your whole position folds."

Juliette looked at the phone. He had a page open, some forum, some rabbi's answer column, and she started to argue on instinct before she caught herself, because that was the trouble with her, she argued first and read second. "Show me the actual text," she said. "Not some guy's summary. I need the source." Tommy raised his eyebrows at her as if to note, for the record, that this was new behavior.

Ms. Morales from next door knocked while they were still hunched over the laptop; she'd come to return the casserole dish, and she lingered in the doorway in her gardening gloves, amused by the paper avalanche. When Juliette explained the debate, Ms. Morales said her late husband had studied this sort of thing and that half his books were still in her garage if they wanted them, come by anytime, and then she left the dish on the counter and went back to her roses. Tommy went out with her and came back carrying two grocery bags of books, one of which smelled like a basement.

It was Jaeden who found it, in an index, of all places, and he read the entry out loud while Juliette went to the shelf for the volume it pointed to. "It's called pikuach nefesh," he read. "Saving a life. It says saving a life overrides the commandments." Juliette turned to the page and read the whole passage herself, twice, because she did not trust a thing until she had held it. The principle was there in the text, older than any car, older than any hospital: saving a human life came before almost everything else, Sabbath included. The uncle could drive. The keys were not the question. The question had never been the keys.

"So I lose," Jaeden said, but he didn't sound like he'd lost. He sounded like he was rechecking the math.

"No," Juliette said slowly. "Look what it actually means. The rule doesn't break. The rule bends around the life, on purpose, from inside." She was aware she was talking faster now, aware of Tommy watching her arrive somewhere. The strictness she'd underlined wasn't the whole of it; there was a second thing underneath, a designed softness, and she'd mistaken rigidity for strength. She wondered whether every old law had a hidden hinge like this, some place where it yielded, and whether finding the hinge was itself a kind of respect. "For the debate," she said, "I take the strict passage, and I take this, and I show they were written by people who understood emergencies exist."

"Which side does that help?" Tommy asked.

"Both," she said, and laughed when both boys groaned. "That's the honest answer. It helps both."

She copied the citation onto an index card in her smallest handwriting, then flipped the card over and wrote a question on the back: what does the rule look like when nothing is at stake? She left it there, unanswered, tucked under the sugar bowl, and went to the counter to slice apples for the three of them while Jaeden read the passage aloud one more time, slowly, testing the words against himself.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Paul Boyer and John Walker shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how ATP synthase makes ATP.
story:
The museum map showed the biology wing as a scattering of green rooms across the third floor, an archipelago of exhibits connected by glass bridges, and Sydney stood at the bottom of the escalator trying to decide which island to visit first. She had until Thursday. Thursday was the unit test, the one Mr. Ferreira had warned them about twice, and cellular respiration was the section she'd bombed on the quiz. She could name the stages, glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, in order, but when the quiz asked where the ATP actually came from, she'd written something vague about energy being released and had lost eleven points for it. Eleven points she needed back.

Jaxson had suggested the museum, partly because his little brother's birthday party had bought them all passes, partly because he claimed he learned better standing up. Lorelei came because she had finished studying already and wanted a smoothie from the café. "You could just read the textbook again," Lorelei said as they rode up, balancing her smoothie. "That's what I did." Sydney said maybe, but reading had been the problem. The words slid past each other like tiles in a puzzle she kept assembling wrong.

The cellular respiration exhibit occupied a dim room with a floor-wide diagram of a cell, and Sydney walked onto it, shoes planted on the cytoplasm, looking down the long corridor toward the mitochondria printed in the corner. Jaxson crouched near the start of it, where a cluster of yellow hexagons represented glucose. "Okay," he said. "So this thing gets broken in half first." She knew that much. Glycolysis split the sugar, spent a little ATP to make more, sent the pieces inward. The diagram made it feel like a journey, and she followed it, step by step, narrating under her breath the way Mr. Ferreira had taught them, glucose to pyruvate, pyruvate to acetyl CoA, the Krebs cycle turning like a wheel over a loading zone, electrons handed off to carriers.

The room was quiet on a weekday afternoon, and for a moment the whole pathway seemed to settle into place in her head, an order she could actually walk through with her body. Then she reached the mitochondrion printed across the far corner and stopped. Inside it the diagram showed a folded inner membrane with a stubby mushroom-shaped structure embedded in it, and beside the structure a single bold label. She read it, then read it again.

"Jaxson. Come look at this."

He ambled over, brother trailing behind him. The label read ATP synthase, and beneath it, in smaller text, a caption about how this enzyme spins as protons stream through it, and how understanding its mechanism had won Paul Boyer and John Walker the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Lorelei drifted over, straw in her mouth. "Wait," she said. "A Nobel Prize? For this little mushroom?"

"For explaining how it makes ATP," Sydney said slowly. She was staring at the shape of the thing, at the tiny rotor drawn in cross-section, turning. All those steps she'd memorized, glucose splitting, the cycle turning, electrons hopping down the transport chain, and here at the end of it all was a machine. Not energy floating free, not some evanescent spark released into the cell, but a literal rotating enzyme, and the ATP was built by the spin of it. "I think I had it backwards," she said. "I thought the chain made the ATP. It doesn't. The chain pushes protons across, and then they flow back through this, and the flow turns it, and the turning assembles the ATP."

Jaxson leaned closer to the cross-section. "So it's like a mill." She nodded, though she could feel the edges of what she didn't understand.
