Why the protons flowed back only through the enzyme, what the rotor actually gripped, how a spin became a bond; the caption didn't say, and she was honest enough with herself to know a museum floor was not going to disabuse her of every misconception by dinnertime. But the shape of the mistake was clear now. She hadn't been missing a fact. She'd been missing the idea that there was a mechanism at the center of it, something you could draw, something two scientists had spent years working out well enough to share a Nobel Prize.

There was a bench nearby with a laminated card and a plastic model of the enzyme, and Sydney sat down and turned the rotor with her finger, watching a notch sweep past three fixed positions. Out, out, out, the little ADP markers clicking into place. She did it again. Jaxson sat beside her and did it once himself, then went to fetch his brother from the gift shop before he spent his birthday money on astronaut ice cream.

Lorelei stood finishing her smoothie, watching Sydney turn the rotor a fourth time. "So Thursday," Lorelei said, "when he asks where the ATP comes from?"

Sydney turned the rotor again, slow, feeling the click of each position under her fingertip. "I'll tell him it's made by a spinning enzyme in the inner membrane," she said, "and if he asks how anyone figured that out, I know that too."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
story:
David had promised his parents a proper dinner at the campsite, not the usual burnt sausages, and he had chosen chicken with a garlic mayonnaise because it sounded impressive and required only a bowl and a fork. His father was out patching the tent pole. His grandmother sat in a folding chair by the fire pit, watching him measure oil into a cup with the concentration of someone watching a card game she had money on.

The first minutes went well. He broke a yolk into the bowl, added a spoon of vinegar, and began dripping oil while whisking, the way the recipe on his phone said, slowly, slowly. The mixture turned pale and thick, and he felt a small pride he did not say aloud. Then Lohan texted him a photo of a fish he had caught at another lake, forty minutes north, and the caption read "come up tonight, drayden's here, we're staying til sunday." David read it twice with the fork still in his hand, and in that unwatched moment he poured the oil too fast. The sauce let go of itself. It thinned, then turned glassy, and a yellow pool of oil rose to the top while a sad watery liquid sank beneath it.

"Grandma," he said. "It broke."

She leaned forward and looked at the bowl the way a nurse looks at a patient. "Whisk it harder," she said, which he did, for a full minute, and it only got worse, the oil swimming in separate shining beads that refused to join anything.

He wanted to dump it out and start over, but they had brought exactly six eggs and his father had already used two at breakfast. Dumping it meant no sauce, and no sauce meant admitting the whole dinner had been a performance. Lohan's message sat on the phone screen. He typed back "maybe" and put the phone face down on the picnic table.

His grandmother went to the trailer and came back with a battered tin box, the kind that had once held cookies. Inside were folded papers, and she pulled one out and handed it to him. It was in his grandfather's handwriting, a letter he had written her the summer before they married, from a fishing camp not far from this one. The middle paragraphs were about missing her, and David read those quickly, embarrassed, but the last paragraph changed subject entirely. In mayonnaise, the letter said, lecithin and proteins from the egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate. That was the whole trick. That was why you added the oil slowly, drop by drop, giving those substances time to wrap each droplet and keep it held. It was also, his grandfather had written under a drawing of a bowl, the reason a broken mayonnaise could be brought back: you gave it a fresh yolk and fed the old oil to it again, gently, as if the whole thing had never failed.

"It's how you resuscitate it," his grandmother said. "Your grandfather taught me the year we were engaged. I ruined it three times in one week and he never once laughed." She said "emulsifiers" the way she said "paracetamol," like a word that lived in kitchens.

David separated another egg, keeping the yolk whole in his palm, and slid it into a clean bowl. He whisked the yolk alone until it was sticky and uniform, then, going slower than he had ever done anything, he began adding the split sauce a teaspoon at a time, spoon by spoon, watching for the moment when it would either work or humiliate him. Around the third spoonful the mixture tightened. It climbed the tines of the fork. He kept going, half speed, and the entire failed bowl folded back into something glossy and thick and standing in soft peaks, as though nothing had ever gone wrong with it at all.

His father came back from the tent pole and stood at the table with his hands in his pockets. "Smells like a restaurant," he said, which was not quite true of raw garlic and oil, but David took it. He was thinking, as he whisked, about how the failure and the fix were the same substance, the same yolk doing the same work, and how the second attempt had only succeeded because the first one existed to be fed into it. He could not decide whether that meant anything beyond eggs. He suspected it did not. He suspected it might.

The phone buzzed again. Lohan: "drayden says you're scared of the fish." David looked at the bowl, then at the fire pit, where his grandmother had begun laying out the chicken pieces. It was a two-hour drive north, the roads would be dark by nine, and his parents would either say yes with that flat voice that meant no, or say no with the voice that meant ask again in the morning. He picked up the fork, tasted the sauce, and found it better than the first one had been.

"Needs more lemon," his grandmother said, handing him half of one, already cut.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation.
story:
The campsite sat on a riparian shelf above the river, close enough that Benjamin could hear water moving under the sound of the fire. He had brought his Earth science binder because Ms. Li had agreed to a retake on Monday, and because his father had said, in the car, that a camping trip was no excuse. The retake covered greenhouse gases and the carbon dioxide record, and Benjamin had failed the first attempt by writing, in confident pencil, that the most common gases in the air must trap the most heat.

He said as much now, holding the binder near the flames for light. "Nitrogen and oxygen are like ninety-nine percent of the air," he said. "So most of the trapped heat comes from them. That's just logic."

Bronwyn, who had come along because Mia had come along, lowered her marshmallow and looked at him the way she looked at wrong answers in study hall. "That's not logic," she said. "That's an assumption wearing logic's jacket." She took the binder from him, flipped pages with sticky fingers, and turned it around so the firelight caught a paragraph. "Read the bold part."

He read it. Nitrogen and oxygen made up about 99 percent of dry air but were not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms did not absorb infrared radiation. He read it twice. The most abundant things in the sky, the stuff he breathed without thinking, let heat pass straight through, and the whole trouble came from the trace leftovers, the parts per million.

"So the air is mostly made of gases that do nothing," Mia said from her camp chair, sounding personally offended by this. "The atmosphere is a fraud."

"It's not a fraud," Benjamin said. "It's selective." He was already looking at the graph, the one that climbed in a slow sawtooth and then bent upward, decade over decade. Before, the line had been a shape to memorize. Now it meant something stranger: a fraction so small you could ignore it, and you couldn't ignore it.

That night the temperature dropped fast, the way it did when the sky was clear, and his father made a joke about being grateful the heat wasn't all escaping tonight, and Benjamin explained, haltingly, why the joke worked better than his father knew. Nitrogen and oxygen, two identical atoms, no infrared absorption, 99 percent of dry air. His father said "huh" in the tone of a man filing something away.

At breakfast, Mia handed him a folded page torn from her notebook. "You weren't awake when I wrote it," she said. "Don't read it until you're alone, and don't be weird about it."

He walked down to the riverbank and unfolded it. Dear Benjamin, the note began, like a letter even though she was forty meters away. You said last night that the retake isn't fair because some people got tutors and you got a weekend in the woods. Maybe. But Ms. Li isn't running a meritocracy where the rich kids win automatically. She's giving you a second chance to show what you actually understand, and last night you understood it. I watched you figure out that graph in real time. Also, Bronwyn says the unit after this one is ocean currents, and the currents are destabilizing because of fresh meltwater, so don't get comfortable. Study the graph tonight. We will quiz you with s'mores as the stakes. Your friend, which is a real thing and not a consolation prize, Mia.

He folded the note and put it in the binder, between the unit he'd failed and the one coming.

They did quiz him, by lantern, with the s'mores, and he answered everything, and when he got to the part about nitrogen and oxygen he drew the two identical atoms in the dirt with a stick and said, "These don't absorb infrared. That's why the biggest part of the air isn't the problem." Mia awarded him a marshmallow. The graph he could now read like a sentence, sawtooth and all, the breath of the whole planet drawn once a year, each year's line a little higher than the last.

The next morning a woman came down from the site above theirs, borrowing sugar, and stood talking to his father by the cold fire pit while Benjamin repacked the binder. She asked what the trip was for, and his father pointed at him and said, retake prep, greenhouse effect, and the woman turned out to be a teacher too, and before Benjamin quite knew how it happened she was standing next to him at the picnic table asking him to explain it, testing him the way teachers do, gently, with her arms crossed.

He took a breath and explained the whole thing, the 99 percent, the identical atoms, the trace gases doing all the work, the climbing graph and what its axes meant, and he kept his voice steady and he did not stop early, and when he finished he felt the particular brightness of having actually said something true.

The woman nodded slowly. "That's a better explanation than the one I gave my class on Tuesday," she said. "What subject do you teach?" Benjamin asked, and she smiled. "P.E.," she said. "I coach swimming." She picked up her sugar and walked back up the hill, and Benjamin sat down at the picnic table and started to laugh.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: Automation bias is the tendency to favor suggestions from automated systems and to ignore contradicting information, even when that information is correct.
story:
The essay was due at midnight, and by seven o'clock Zachary had written the same paragraph four times. His laptop sat open on the corner table of Mr. Cho's coffee shop, where the wifi was free and the owner let students stay past closing if they kept their cups on the saucers. The prompt was simple enough to be humiliating: describe an ethical problem raised by technology, using a concrete example. He had chosen algorithmic bias, mostly because Maverick had chosen surveillance and Braiden had chosen automation, and Zachary refused to write the same paper as anyone at their lunch table.

He was on his fifth attempt when the trouble started at the kiosk. Mr. Cho had installed it in September, a touchscreen that took orders and payments so the single human behind the counter could focus on making drinks. A woman in a rain jacket ordered a latte, paid with her card, and then the screen told her, in cheerful gray type, that her payment had been declined. The barista, whose name tag said Dana, leaned over her own terminal and said, "It actually went through on my end. I can see it right here."

"That's all right," the woman said, already swiping her card again at the kiosk, because the kiosk had told her to.

Zachary watched her pay twice. Dana watched it too, and then had to walk the woman through the refund process, which the kiosk did not offer, because the kiosk was certain nothing was wrong. Mr. Cho came out from the back, wiping his hands, and Zachary braced himself to watch the man lambaste the machine, which he did, at length and in two languages, but the machine absorbed the abuse without changing its behavior, which struck Zachary as a very modern form of power.

"It's called automation bias," said Maverick, who had appeared with his own laptop and a muffin he intended to make last the whole evening. He had a mannerism of pointing with his chin, and he pointed it now at the woman's receipt. "People trust the system over the person standing right in front of them. Even when the person is right." Maverick had been researching surveillance all week and had apparently accumulated everyone else's vocabulary along the way.

Zachary typed the phrase and then stopped, because the phrase was suddenly not abstract. The woman had ignored Dana's terminal, the correct information, delivered by a human with a face, in favor of gray type on a screen. Dana had the refund working inside of four minutes, and when the woman thanked her, Dana said, "It happens about five times a week," in the flat voice of someone who had stopped expecting to be believed.

But Zachary, watching Dana sort it out, found himself unwilling to write the easy paper, the one where the machine was the villain. Mr. Cho had bought the kiosk because he couldn't afford a second employee, and it had kept the shop open, which meant it had kept Dana's job existing at all, in however reduced a form. And the woman in the rain jacket had not been stupid. She had probably been tired, and the kiosk had been confident, and confidence was easier to follow than a stranger's word. When Braiden texted asking whether automation would destroy employment entirely, Zachary wrote back that the woman's double charge seemed more pernicious than job loss, in its quiet way, and then deleted the sentence, because he wasn't sure it was true, only that it felt true.

At ten, Dana brought him a shortbread cookie he hadn't ordered and set it down without comment, the way you do for someone who has been typing for three hours and eaten one muffin's worth of nothing. Mr. Cho locked the front door at eleven and left the back light on for the students. Zachary wrote the paragraph about the woman and the kiosk, then a paragraph about Dana's terminal, then a paragraph admitting he didn't know whether the answer was better software, a second employee, or customers willing to argue with gray type. At 11:54 he read it over and found it less finished than honest.

He hit submit at 11:58. Maverick was asleep on his own laptop, chin on his chin-pointing fist, and Braiden was still texting paragraphs about robot cashiers. Zachary closed the lid, pocketed the last corner of cookie, and carried his cup and saucer to the counter, where Dana was wrapping the pastries for tomorrow.

"You believed me," Dana said. "First one all night."

"You had the terminal," Zachary said, and Dana laughed and slid him the last unsold croissant across the counter.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: High blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all, which is why it is called a silent killer and is found mainly by measuring it.
story:
Maelie set the borrowed cuff on her grandmother's kitchen table, between the dish rack and a bowl of green beans still waiting to be topped and tailed. The machine belonged to the school nurse, who had agreed to lend it for the weekend after Mr. Ramos assigned the health unit, and Maelie had signed her name on the little sticker in careful letters, the way one signs for something that matters more than it looks.

Her grandmother swept beans into the sink and ran the water. "You can practice on me," she said, "but you will find nothing. I feel fine, so my pressure is fine."

Maelie had read otherwise. She had read it twice, on Thursday night, in the chapter Mr. Ramos had assigned, while Sophia sent her messages about Marc-Antoine and the party and whether he had actually meant what he said about the ocean. She slid the cuff up her grandmother's arm, tightened the velcro until it held without pinching, and pressed the button. The machine hummed, swelled, released.

"One sixty-two over ninety-four," Maelie read.

Her grandmother dried her hands on the dish towel and looked out the window, where the gray water of the cove lay flat as a lid. She lived in this littoral town all her life, two streets up from the boats, and she cooked with salt the way her own mother had, and her mother before her, a genealogy of heavy hands with the shaker that nobody in the family had ever thought to question. "The machine is wrong," she said, but she said it to the window, not to Maelie.

"It might be," Maelie said. "Let's do it again."

The second reading was nearly the same. The third, after her grandmother had sat still for five minutes with her feet flat on the floor the way the chapter said, barely moved. Maelie turned the notebook toward her, where she had written the numbers down in a column, because Mr. Ramos wanted them to track something real over the weekend and bring the data in on Monday. Marc-Antoine was tracking his little brother's screen time. Sophia was tracking her own sleep. Maelie had thought, when she chose, that she was picking the easy option.

"You feel fine, though," Maelie said slowly. She was not arguing; she was working it out, the way she did in the margins of a math problem. "That's the thing. I read that it usually causes no symptoms at all. That's why they call it the silent killer. Nobody finds it by feeling it. They find it by measuring it."

Her grandmother sat down in the chair she always sat in, the one nearest the stove, and pressed her thumb along the seam of the towel. Outside, a gull dropped something on the rocks and dropped it again. "Your grandfather," she said finally, "felt fine the whole winter before his stroke."

Maelie had not known that. The fact she had read in the chapter and the fact sitting across the table were two different shapes, and she turned them against each other in silence. One was a sentence in a book. The other was her grandmother's hands going still on the towel.

"Monday I have to explain," Maelie said, "how diet and exercise change it. Not why. Just that they do." She looked at the bowl of beans, the salt cellar beside it, the butter dish. "Could we try something this weekend? Less salt. Walk down to the wharf in the mornings. I'll measure you every day and write it down. If the numbers don't move, I'll say that too. I don't want to tell the class a nice story if the numbers say something boring."

Her grandmother laughed, a short, surprised sound. "You want to experiment on your grandmother."

"I want to be honest about what I find," Maelie said. "Mr. Ramos said half of science is being willing to be wrong."

They ate the beans that night with almost no salt, and her grandmother complained twice and ate them anyway. In the morning they walked down to the wharf while the fog was still burning off the water, and the fishermen nodded at them, and the machine hummed on her grandmother's arm at the kitchen table while the kettle came to a boil.

"One fifty-four," Maelie read, and wrote it in the column, and underlined nothing.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A guitar in standard tuning has its six strings tuned, from lowest to highest, to E, A, D, G, B and E.
story:
The guitar had belonged to Abigail's grandfather, and it came to the community center in a case that smelled like the inside of a drawer. Ms. Ong had cleared the back room for the Saturday lessons, between the folding tables and the mural someone had started years ago and never finished, a sky that ended in primer gray halfway across the wall.

"Strings first," Ms. Ong said, and then she was called away to deal with a flooded sink in the kitchen, which was how Abigail ended up alone with the instrument and Melodie, who had come ostensibly to do homework.

"It's all wrong," Abigail said, plucking the lowest string. She had a tuner app on her phone, a green needle that swung left when a note was flat. "Every single string."

"Maybe that's a sign," Melodie said, not looking up from her chemistry notes. "Maybe take up the recorder."

Abigail ignored this. The lowest string wanted to be an E, and the app told her it was somewhere below that, sagging, so she tightened the peg a little at a time, the way you'd turn a tap you didn't trust. The needle crept right and settled. E. Then the next string up wanted A, which struck her as odd, because the note after E, if you were counting letters, would be F. She said so.

"It skips," Melodie said. "It's not the alphabet, it's music. Letters are parochial that way."

"Letters aren't parochial. Countries are parochial."

"Fine. Then the alphabet is parochial. Keep turning."

D came next, then G, and by the fourth string Abigail had begun to feel the logic of it, or at least the shape of the logic, the way the letters climbed and then, on the last string, dropped back down to an E that was higher than the first. From lowest to highest it ran E, A, D, G, B, and E again, a fact she hadn't known an hour ago and now owned like a small coin in her pocket. She played the six open strings in a row. It wasn't a song. It was more like reciting something, and it made her want to laugh.

Malika arrived halfway through, wet from the walk, holding a folded piece of paper she'd apparently been given by someone at the front desk. "This is for you," she said. "The guy said you left your number on the sign-up sheet."

The note was from the front desk volunteer, a retired man Abigail had spoken to once. She unfolded it. If your grandfather's guitar is the Yamaha I think it is, I played in a band with a man who had one just like it, 1974, at a hall four streets from here. I tuned it then and it held. Those strings remember. Come find me Tuesdays.

"He knows my grandfather's guitar," Abigail said, and read it aloud, and Malika said, "That's either beautiful or slightly eerie," and Melodie said, "Both, probably," and Abigail folded the note carefully along its original creases and put it in the case's side pocket, where it would ride with the picks.

What she did not say, because she was still turning it over, was that she had wanted the guitar to be broken. That was the honest and ugly part. If it were broken, or wrong, or beyond her, then quitting it would be reasonable rather than cowardly. Her mother had started a rapprochement with the grandfather last spring, after six years of not speaking, and Abigail had not decided how she felt about being handed his instrument in the middle of that thaw. People valorize forgiveness in her family the way some people valorize grudges, loudly and without detail, and she suspected both were easier to praise than to practice.

"Play something," Malika said, settling onto a folding chair.

"I know four chords and half of them badly."

"So play the bad half."

Abigail put her fingers where the lesson sheet showed, an E minor shape, and strummed, and the strings buzzed against the frets, and she adjusted, and strummed again, and this time it rang, the two E's at either end of the tuning like bookends with D and G and B shelved between them. She switched to the next chord and missed, and Malika said nothing with her whole face, which was louder than saying something.

Melodie closed her chemistry notes. "My mom wants me to quit coming to these," she said, to the mural, to the gray half of the sky. "She thinks Saturdays should be for the internship applications."

"What do you think?"

"I think I like it here. I like that it's loud and nothing's due." Melodie looked at her hands. "But she's not wrong that I have to apply places. Both things can be true. That's the annoying part."

Abigail nodded slowly. She strummed the E minor again, then moved one finger and it became G, and the change was small enough that she almost missed having made it. On Tuesday she would find the man from the front desk and ask him what hall, what year, what her grandfather had been like with a guitar in his hands, and she would listen to whatever he remembered. She did not know yet whether she would tell her mother. That was the part that stayed uncertain, the string not yet tuned.

She ran the six open strings once more, low to high, listening for the two E's.

"What's that called," Malika asked, "when you play them all open like that?"

"Nothing," Abigail said. "It's just E, A, D, G, B, and E."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: In 1854, physician John Snow mapped cholera deaths in London and showed they clustered around one water pump on Broad Street, an early example of spatial analysis.
story:
The lab was supposed to close at five, but Mr. Pérez had stayed late every night that week, and by Thursday the room smelled of marker pens and the vending machine dinners Kevin had stopped pretending were food. On the projector, the city map glowed in layers he had built himself: census blocks in pale orange, the hundred-year floodplain in blue, and where they overlapped, an ugly bruise of purple that spread across the east side like a spill no one had mopped.

The deadline was Friday morning, first period, the regional showcase. Kevin had two problems. The first was technical, a boundary file that refused to align, so his floodplain sat forty meters off from the parcels underneath it. The second was worse. Myla had looked at his draft slides the night before and said, "It's just a picture of purple. So what? You need to tell people why anyone ever thought to put a map on top of another map."

He had been turning that over all day, half-listening in chemistry, sketching in the margin of his notes. After school he found Frederik in the library copying homework he claimed was merely "reference material," and Kevin sat down across from him without asking. "I need a beginning," he said. "Like an origin story for what I'm doing."

"Maps have origin stories now," Frederik said, not looking up.

Kevin turned his notebook sideways so Frederik could see what he'd written. "There's this thing I found. In 1854, a physician named John Snow mapped cholera deaths in London, and the deaths clustered around one water pump on Broad Street." He tapped the page. "One pump. That was basically the first spatial analysis. People were dying and nobody could see the pattern until he drew it."

"So your project is the cholera pump," Frederik said.

"My project is the pump, but with floods and apartments instead." Kevin felt the sentence settle somewhere behind his ribs, the way a proof does when the last line finally connects. He had spent weeks thinking the software was the point, the layers, the coordinate systems, the tedious clipping of shapefiles. Now he understood the software was only the instrument, and the argument was the thing. The purple bruise was an argument: that the city had allowed, maybe even encouraged, housing to concentrate exactly where the water would go.

He went back to the lab at four. Mr. Pérez was at his desk grading with the weary asceticism of a man who had given up coffee for Lent two weeks early, and Kevin asked about the boundary file. Together they found the projection error, a mismatch buried in a properties menu neither of them had thought to open, and the layers snapped together with a soft click that Kevin would have sworn was audible. He spent the next hour internalizing what he'd done wrong, repeating the steps in his head so he could find it again without help, and while he worked he kept talking, because Mr. Pérez had asked what the project was for.

"People build where it's cheap," Kevin said, dragging the pointer along the river. "And it's cheap where it floods, because nobody with money chooses the floodplain. So the overlay isn't just geography. It's about who the city decided could live in the purple." Mr. Pérez didn't answer right away, which Kevin had learned was how he showed approval.

At six, Myla appeared in the doorway with two plastic bags, munificent beyond all reason: sandwiches, chocolate, a jar of instant coffee. "You're going to present on four hours of sleep otherwise," she said, setting them down. "Show me the new version." Kevin ran the slides. Broad Street and the pump first, then the blue and the orange and the bruise, then the table of buildings, and Myla nodded slowly and said, "There's one thing you can't answer, though. Who's your data from, and are you going to pretend it's perfect?" Kevin looked at the map. The flood layer was a model, an estimate, a probability; the census was five years old; the purple was true and also uncertain, both at once, and he had forty dollars of printer credit and one night. "Then I'll put a slide about what I don't know," he said, and started typing.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: For US federal Direct Subsidized student loans, the government pays the interest while the student is in school; unsubsidized loans build interest during that time.
story:
Sienna had chosen the credit union because it was empty at four in the afternoon and because the pamphlet rack stood where no teller could see her face while she read. She held two financial aid letters side by side, one from State and one from a small college two states east, and a pamphlet titled "Understanding Interest" that seemed to have been designed by someone who hated teenagers.

"Are you hiding?" Heather slid in beside her at the pamphlet rack, backpack still on.

"I'm deliberating." Sienna tapped the letters. "Both gave me federal Direct loans. State's is subsidized. The other one gave me part subsidized, part unsubsidized. And I don't fully know what that changes."

Heather picked up a pamphlet about reverse mortgages, looked at it the way one looks at a dead bird, and put it back. "My mom says loans are a scam invented to monetize your twentieth birthday. That's her whole financial literacy."

Behind them, at the counter, Mr. Rivera was arguing about a certificate of deposit. He coached freshman soccer and lived three doors down, and he had opinions about everything, delivered at volume. "I put money in, it sits there, it grows," he was saying to the teller. "That's the whole arrangement. I'm not asking it to dance."

Sienna turned the State letter over. In the fine print she found a line she'd skimmed three times: for the subsidized loan, the government pays the interest while she was in school. The unsubsidized ones were different; they built interest during that time, quietly, while she was writing essays and failing to monetize anything at all. She read the line twice, then looked at the other letter's numbers as if they'd been rearranged behind her back.

"Wait," she said. "So the subsidized one just doesn't grow while I'm in classes? The government covers it?"

"If that's what it says," Heather said. "Don't ask me. My plan is to marry rich and diversify later."

"You could diversify now."

"My talents don't lend themselves to early diversification."

Nicholas came through the door shaking rain off his jacket, saw them, and made the face of someone who had hoped the credit union would be empty. "You're doing the loan thing," he said. "In public. Voluntarily."

"I'm comparing offers," Sienna said. "State's subsidized. The other school mixes subsidized with unsubsidized, and the unsubsidized part is already piling up interest while I'd be enrolled."

"That's why everyone says subsidized is the good one," Nicholas said, as though this were common knowledge he'd been storing for exactly this moment. He had not known it last week, when he'd asked her what "FAFSA" stood for and guessed wrong twice.

At the counter, Mr. Rivera concluded his business. "Four percent," he announced to the room, to no one and everyone. "My savings earn four percent now. Money sitting still, doing nothing, earning more than my first job." He collected his receipt with the satisfaction of a man who had personally defeated economics.

"That's savings," Sienna said, mostly to herself. "Interest works on savings too. Same mechanism, opposite direction. One grows your money, the other grows what you owe."

"Deep," said Nicholas.

"It's not deep, it's arithmetic, and I've been treating it like a travesty of justice all week when really I just didn't read page three." She squared the two letters. The small college had given her more aid overall, more of everything, including more of the kind that charged her to attend while she was attending. State's package was smaller and quieter. She stood there a long moment holding both, aware that she was choosing between a bigger door and a cheaper one, and that she could not actually know which hallway led where.

"So which one?" Heather asked.

"State, probably. Because of the subsidized part." Sienna slid the letters into her backpack. "Probably."

Mr. Rivera paused at the door on his way out. "You three opening accounts? Compound interest, start now. Best thing I ever did was put away two hundred dollars at your age."

Heather looked at him with genuine interest. "And it grew into?"

He held up his receipt, examined it, and put it back in his pocket. "Into a certificate," he said, and walked out into the rain.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Japan has one of the world's oldest populations, with about 29 percent of its people aged 65 or over in the early 2020s.
story:
The departure board still said ON TIME for the flight to Tokyo, so Mackenzie spread her notebook across two seats at the gate and tried, for the third time, to make the population pyramid obey her. Ms. Lin had handed out the assignment on the last day of term, a photocopy of Japan's pyramid with its wide base from the 1950s narrowing to almost nothing, and the question underneath: what does a country build when its shape looks like this, schools or nursing homes? Mackenzie was supposed to answer it before she landed. Ten months of exchange, and this was the price of leaving early, the homework that traveled with her.

"Kenzie, you're going to get graphite poisoning," Alana said, dropping into the seat beside her with two teas. She slid one across. "Drink. Your hand is shaking."

"It's a pyramid, it's not even hard math, it's just bars." Mackenzie pressed so hard the pencil snapped. Salma leaned over from the other side and picked up the broken half without comment, sharpened it with the little blade on her keychain, and set it back on the notebook like an offering. That was Salma; she never made a thing of helping. Mackenzie breathed out and looked at the shape again. Japan had one of the world's oldest populations, the textbook page said, with about 29 percent of its people aged 65 or over in the early 2020s. She'd underlined it twice on the train to the airport and then felt vaguely guilty, as if underlining a number could absolve her of having ignored everything else on the page.

"I thought old meant, like, temples," Alana said, reading over her shoulder. "I didn't know a country could be old the way a person is."

"Twenty-nine percent," Mackenzie said. "Of everyone. That's not temples, that's ramps and clinics and people to lift people." She said it and then heard it, and the pyramid suddenly stopped being abstract bars and became the street outside her host family's apartment in Sendai, which she had walked through once on a video call, all narrow sidewalks and handrails. "So the answer's nursing homes. Obviously. It's not even a question."

Salma was quiet for a moment, blowing on her tea. "My grandmother lives in Alexandria," she said finally. "And when my uncle wanted to put her in a home, the whole building signed a petition against it. Caring for her was everyone's job, not an institution's. It's partly sectarian there, which family and which church takes which old person, but it meant she was never alone." She shrugged. "I'm not saying Japan is Egypt. I'm saying the bars don't tell you who does the lifting."

Mackenzie started to argue, then didn't. She looked at her notebook, at the answer she'd been so sure of, the one she'd planned to write in the first five minutes of the flight and then sleep for eleven hours. Nursing homes. But Salma's grandmother was in the bars too, somewhere, and no bar recorded a petition, or a neighbor who carried groceries upstairs, or the fact that a country could answer its own shape in a hundred different ways. Ms. Lin's question was a trap disguised as arithmetic, and Mackenzie had walked straight into it holding a pencil.

The gate agent announced preboarding for passengers needing assistance, and an old man two rows ahead rose slowly, one hand on his wife's elbow, his other hand occupied by a small boy's grip, a grandson maybe, swinging a dinosaur. The three of them moved together toward the jetway, the boy chattering about a vaccine he'd gotten for school and how it had put "a dead antigen" in his arm on purpose, which his grandfather clearly found hilarious. Mackenzie watched them until the jetway swallowed them, then wrote, under her crossed-out answer, a new line: the pyramid tells you what a country has a lot of; it does not tell you what the country will do about it.

"That's not an answer," Alana said, reading it.

"It's the honest one. I'll say nursing homes are the likelier guess, twenty-nine percent means the pressure is real, and then I'll say I want to see who's actually doing the work before I decide." Mackenzie closed the notebook and put it in her carry-on, on top of her passport. When her group was called, Salma hugged her first, then Alana, longer, and pressed a granola bar into the side pocket of her bag where Mackenzie would find it somewhere over the Pacific. At the jetway door Mackenzie turned around once and waved, and Alana mouthed something that was either good luck or goodbye, and Mackenzie walked on.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month.
story:
Hudson's mother had signed him up before he could argue, the way she signed him up for things, so on the last Saturday before senior year he stood in the kitchen at seven in the morning eating toast over the sink while she read the confirmation email aloud. Two shifts a month, it said, Saturdays, nine to one, the church basement on Bellwood. He said fine. She said it would be good for his college applications, and he said fine again, and then she said something about giving back and he put his plate in the dishwasher and left before she could finish the sentence.

Yousef was already on the church steps, hood up, scrolling his phone. "You too?" he said when Hudson came up the walk. "My mom and your mom talked." The line outside the basement door went down the steps and along the sidewalk, past the pharmacy, and Yousef kept turning his head to look at it. "It's Saturday morning," he said. "People are sleeping in. Why is it this long on a Saturday?"

Inside, a man named Mr. Marino handed them clipboards and put them at a folding table by the door. Their job was to record household sizes on intake forms, then collate the forms into stacks of ten for the coordinator, who would enter them later on the office computer. It was not difficult work. Mr. Marino showed them once, watched them do two forms, and moved off to argue with a delivery driver about a pallet of dented cans.

The line moved slowly and the basement filled with the noise of it, children, a radio someone had brought, cart wheels on linoleum. Hudson wrote down numbers: two, four, one, three. A woman with a toddler on her hip gave her name and spelled it twice because he had it wrong the first time, and when he apologized she said it was fine, everyone spells it wrong, and did not smile. After the third stack of forms, he stopped looking up when people approached. It was faster that way, and the line was longer than anyone had planned for, and being fast felt like the only useful thing he could be.

Yousef had stopped writing. He was reading a poster taped to the wall behind the intake table, the kind nobody looks at, with a bar chart on it. "Hudson," he said. "Look at this." Hudson said he was in the middle of a form. "Look at it." Hudson finished the form, clipped it, and turned. The poster said Food Banks Canada, HungerCount 2025, and beneath the chart a line of small text he had to lean in to read. "Nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025," Yousef read aloud, dragging a finger under the words. "A record for a single month." He looked at the line going out the door and then at the poster and then at the line again. "That was one month. In the whole country."

"So?"

"So that's not a record like, good job. That's a record like worst ever." Yousef's voice had risen, and the woman at the table in front of them glanced over. Mr. Marino appeared behind them, quiet the way he seemed to arrive everywhere quietly, and took the poster's corner between two fingers as if checking whether it was still stuck. "March," he said. "Month like any other." Then he went back to the pallet, and they could hear him telling the driver that dented cans were fine, punctured ones were not, and there was a difference, and the driver did not sound convinced.

They worked through the noon hour. When the line thinned, Yousef started talking again, lower now, about his cousin, who had been in trouble twice and was out now and doing warehouse work. His cousin's counselor used a word for people going back: recidivism. Yousef liked the word, said it felt like a physics term, something with a rate you could measure. He wondered out loud whether there was a word for people coming back to a food bank, whether it was the same kind of thing or a different kind of thing entirely, and Hudson said the forms would tell you, sort of, because half the names on them were probably repeats, and then he heard himself and stopped. He had been writing those names for four hours and had not once thought about whether he had written them before.

He tried to hold both ideas at once on the walk home, and did not manage it. One was his mother's, which she had never said in these words but which felt axiomatic in their house: you give back, you show up, the applications get stronger, the world grades you on it. The other was Yousef's, which was not even an argument, just a number on a poster and a line around a block. If the number was a record, then people showing up to volunteer, himself included, was not the thing that was working. Maybe it was still worth doing. He could not see how to check that, and it seemed dishonest to pretend he could.

His mother was in the kitchen when he got in, and she asked how it went, and he stood in the doorway with his coat still on. "Long line," he said. She waited for more. "There were over two million visits in March," he said. "In the whole country. It was a record." She said that was terrible, that it was a shame, that people were really struggling out there, and she turned back to the stove, and he understood that she had heard the number the way you hear weather. He hung his coat on the hook and sat down at the table without being asked, and the second shift was already circled on the calendar by the fridge, two Saturdays away, in her handwriting.
